Katalog Berita (Halaman 38/57)

#3926. In a reveal that might worry eventual PC players glancing at their GPUs, GTA 6 will target 30fps on all consoles

Oh, and and it'll be streamable on the Xbox One before it's playable on PC

In a press release coinciding with Grand Theft Auto VI becoming available for pre-load ahead of its November 19th release date, Rockstar has confirmed that the game "has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits." Read between the lines, and you can kind of make out the words "...so hope your PCs are up to spec, computer nerds."

GTA 6, of course, still does not have a confirmed PC version, even if Rockstar's former tech director says it's probably not far off. And despite this, even ancient, last-gen consoles are getting in on it, as the release also unexpectedly confirms that the game will be playable on Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming, Microsoft's game streaming service that has suddenly lost its ability to work on PC. Granted, this comes with a warning: "as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay." If you ended up getting a PS4 last generation, no cloud play for you either, I'm afraid. It also states that it will "play best on Playstation 5 consoles", making great use of that Sony partnership, and will include Playstation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows on PS5 Pro.

A 2026 current-gen game targeting 30fps, let alone one as titanic of a release as GTA VI, is probably not going to go down well with a lot of people, even if console players are traditionally les sensitive about FPS counts than PC players. What this does imply, though, is that the inevitable PC release might be an even more demanding behemoth than expected, if Xbox Series and PS5 versions can't even target 60fps. The availability of the game on Xbox One, even if just through cloud streaming, could have resulted in an acceptance that 60fps just wasn't going to be possible if it was also going to be able to 'run' on last-gen hardware. Either way, when it does eventually escape console exclusivity, hopefully trying to run GTA VI on anything less than an RTX 5080 won't set your PC on fire. Now, let me just quickly have a glance at GPU prices. Oh, no.

#3925. UK's Health Service Issues Warning Over GTA 6, Urges Players to Take Care of Their Hands

GTA 6 is so massive that even the UK's National Health Service — commonly known as the NHS — has gotten in on the act.

To be fair, the NHS raises a good point with regards to the open world game's imminent release. On Instagram, it's urging players to take regular breaks in order to avoid issues like repetitive strain injury — or RSI for short.

In a cruel twist, the official account's admin has actually had to undergo surgery to fix their problem, meaning that playing GTA 6 at launch is going to be difficult.

"Thoughts and prayers for your admin. Bit of surgery to remove a lump. Great NHS service, bad timing," the post reads.

"Planning on dedicating time to gaming later this week? Try and take regular breaks, obviously. And be mindful of RSI," it continues.

In this case, RSI is caused by overuse of certain muscles in the hands and fingers, brought about by repeated actions. It's a pretty common injury amongst gamers, and without wanting to scare you off completely, it can lead to lasting damage if you refuse to properly rest the impacted area.

The NHS has got a whole page on RSI if you want more information.

Have you ever had an RSI? Remember to pause your game in the comments section below.

#3924. Three Big Takeaways From Digital Foundry's GTA 6 Analysis For Xbox Series X|S

The good folks over at Digital Foundry have been sharing their deep dive analysis on the Xbox Series X/S versions of GTA 6 today, presented in the form of a 23-minute video on YouTube, and a separate article over on their website.

Feature GTA 6: PS5 vs PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X and Series S: Which Console Plays Best?

Digital FoundryResolution, performance and visual settings compared.

Looking at both of these, there's a ton of interesting information that's shared about the two Xbox versions of the game, so we thought we'd provide a quick summary of what they think about GTA 6 on Xbox Series X and S.

This is just a summary though, and there's way more context and detail in the video at the bottom of this article.

Digital Foundry reckons that the Xbox Series X version of GTA 6 is a great-looking game for the most part, highlighting things like lighting, reflections and even the incredible hair system, while also pointing out minor downsides such as missing shadows and occasionally blurry appearances. They also reckon that the frame rate generally maintains its 30FPS target, but will slip in busy situations like chases and explosions.

"Generally speaking, the game acquits itself quite well on Microsoft's senior current-gen console. Visual settings seem pretty solid across the board."

The Xbox Series S version is also said to be pretty good in the graphical department, retaining the core features that make GTA 6 such a great game visually. It's the frame rate that bothers DF the most, as it's much more variable and prone to falling below its 30FPS target. That said, it appears to hover around 25-30FPS for the most part.

"Series S offers the loosest 30fps lock, with large portions of the game playing out at frame-rates from the mid to high 20s. Again, it's possible to depress the frame-rate to around 20fps with vehicular destruction. The other consoles do a credible job of hitting 30fps, but Series S often lies in a 25-30fps no-man's-land."

If you're wondering which console is the absolute best to play GTA 6 on, it's unsurprisingly the PS5 Pro. Nevertheless, Digital Foundry says that both the Xbox Series X and the PS5 versions "look and play well" despite their softer image, while the Xbox Series S version is the "hardest to recommend" despite its surprisingly impressive visuals.

"In terms of visual features and performance, the PS5 Pro version is the best option available, with solid frame-rates, 4K-like image quality and a noticeable visual upgrade thanks to ray-traced shadows. However, the game looks and plays well on base PS5 and Xbox Series X as well, despite occasional minor frame-rate drops during regular play and a softer 1440p image. The Series S version of the game is the hardest to recommend, with consistent frame-rate drops to the mid-20s, a 1080p output resolution and a long list of visual cutbacks, though the overall character of the game's visuals still shines through."

Both the video and the website article are totally different from each other, so it's worth watching / reading the pair of them and getting a better idea of how GTA 6 fares across both Xbox consoles (and PS5 for that matter).

In my experience, I've found GTA 6 to be fantastic on Xbox Series X across the board for the most part, and while the Series S version is clearly a little more unstable, I'd wager that most players will still be perfectly happy with it.

#3923. God of War: Ragnarok is reportedly the highest-earning PlayStation Studios game this generation, but Marvel's Spider-Man 2 isn't far behind

God of War: Ragnarok is the generation's best-selling and highest-earning PlayStation Studios game, according to a new report, but the full top 10 list has a few nice surprises.

In the four years since its PS5 release and two years since its PC port, God of War: Ragnarok has reportedly sold just over 20m copies and generated $1.4b in revenue, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. About 27.5 percent of the 15m copies it sold on console came from physical editions, and the action blockbuster apparently sold a further 1.1m this year alone. Not bad, boy.

Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.

Kratos and Atreus only narrowly beat out perhaps the biggest superhero of them all: Marvel's Spider-Man 2, a game that reportedly made a whopping $1.3b off 19.1m copies across PS5 and PC. The Spidey sequel should keep swinging even higher as the years chug on, though - the report states that sales always surge during the holiday months, and this year's big screen behemoth Spider-Man: Brand New Day led to an even bigger spike than usual.

Racing sim royalty Gran Turismo 7 ($841m), bug-squashing phenomenon Helldivers 2 ($786m), robo-dino sequel Horizon: Forbidden West ($485m), vengeful spirit sim Ghost of Yotei ($410m), undead remake The Last of Us Part 1 ($341m), multidimensional romp Ratchet and Clank: Rift Apart ($334m), Stellar Blade ($316m) and delightful throwback Astro Bot ($292m) round out the top 10 games published by PlayStation Studios this generation.

It's worth noting that Helldivers 2 and Stellar Blade were developed by studios outside the PlayStation umbrella, but the console maker still published both upon release. Ghost of Yotei's performance is also particularly impressive since Sucker Punch's sequel has only been out for a year and didn't get the benefit of a PC port, like many of its PS5 siblings. The success couldn't save Sucker Punch from recent layoffs, however.

On PlayStation's decision to kill disc-based physical releases, analyst Rhys Elliott said that the bottom five games in the list together made $281.7m this year alone: "PlayStation wants those numbers to be bigger in the coming years, which is one of the reasons it's killing the disc (alongside the better margins it and publishers get through digital.)"

#3922. Bandai Namco is liquidating Unknown 9: Awakening studio Reflector Entertainment, following multiple previous layoffs since the game's launch

As another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco announced in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening. In its notice, Bandai Namco explains that the reason for the liquidation is due to Reflector not meeting its expectations for "future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation."

The press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year. This is not the first time Reflector has been cut by Bandai, as around a month after the launch of Unknown 9: Awakening and presumably in response to its low sales, 18% of the workforce was laid off. 2025 then saw further redundancies amidst the cancellation of a prospective project, though details on those layoffs were not granted by the company. Unknown 9 was intended to be a transmedia franchise involving the game as well as comic books and novels, but these ambitions never came to pass.

Bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now. A similar process faces Arkane Lyon, which is currently in a purgatory of having been chosen for closure by Microsoft, but temporarily protected by French labor laws that prevent it from being suddenly closed without proper negotiation and procedure.

"My first layoff in 14 years making games"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: Following the publication of this story, Crystal Dynamics reached out with the following statement.

"Crystal Dynamics made a difficult, but necessary business decision to reduce our current studio staff by 8 people. Whenever we phase roles off a project, we make every effort to find new spots for our great colleagues first. Everyone affected receives a full severance package as well as job placement assistance to aid them through this transition. We wish them the best and hope to work together in the future."

Original story: Yet another round of layoffs has apparently gone down at Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics, as developers report that they've been cut from the studio. This is at least the sixth round of layoffs since the studio last shipped an original game.

Multiple developers have posted on LinkedIn about the layoffs, as reported by Vertical Slice. Those include UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards and senior game designer Joshua Mitchell. "After several rounds of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, today it was my turn," Mitchell writes. "My first layoff in 14 years making games."

Also cut is senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, who led the development of "procedural tools used extensively in the creation of Tomb Raider: Catalyst's game world," and "integrated Claude Code into procedural tool development." We already knew that Legacy of Atlantis is being made with AI, and it seems the studio is keen to use similar generative tech in Catalyst – though not keen enough to keep the people responsible for it employed, I guess.

Crystal Dynamics has not shipped a new game since the release of Marvel's Avengers in 2020. Since then, it was acquired by Embracer Group, a parent company that's undergone no shortage of financial upheaval in recent years. In 2023, Embracer insisted that Crystal Dynamics would be unaffected by the ongoing layoffs at the broader company, a few months before laying off people at the Tomb Raider studio.

Counting today's cuts, there have been five more rounds of layoffs since then. There were three sets of cuts in 2025 alone, both before and after Perfect Dark – which Crystal Dynamics had been co-developing – was cancelled at Xbox. The studio insisted it was still "fully committed" to its upcoming Tomb Raider games when it announced yet more layoffs in March 2026.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

The extent of today's cuts are not yet fully clear, nor is their effect on the new games. All three developers who've posted about the layoffs so far listed Catalyst among their credits.

#3920. Company of Heroes 3 developer admits "it was a lot" to make the 3.0 overhaul patch alongside regular updates, singleplayer DLC, and a whole spinoff game

The Company of Heroes 3's 3.0 update is huge. Touching virtually every part of the three-year-old RTS, the patch notes are longer than, well, my arm isn't a great measure of patch note length. Let's just say the headline features of overhauled VFX and audio don't really cover it. It also comes with new autumn and winter biomes, an updated grand strategy campaign, improvements to unit AI, and a whole host of other changes.

Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 update's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.

The team began planning the 3.0 update two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Company of Heroes 3, and focus on issues players had flagged since launch. "The VFX were called out," executive producer Denise Christie tells me. "Same thing with a lot of our audio."

Relic were already releasing patches every three months, but the changes they were looking at were much too large for those smaller updates. If they had tried to do the work as part of the small updates, approaching the problems with piecemeal solutions, it would have turned Company of Heroes 3 into a hodgepodge of new and old assets. "We wanted to make sure it was a cohesive package," principal designer Eric Wrobel says. "If you increase the quality of one thing, you have to do it equally across so much stuff." Otherwise you end up with "One that looks awesome and one that's like, 'Oh, this one's kind of gross'."

Complicating matters, though, was that the team couldn't down tools and focus on just these large changes. As well as the small patches that were still going out every three months, both the VFX and audio teams were also contributing the battlegroup DLC packs which added new units to the game. "They would work on stuff and in one branch that was the 3.0 work and then they would go ahead and do some battlegroup stuff and come back to that," Christie says. "It was a lot."

As the 3.0 update grew in scope, it also meant other departments were contributing to the anniversary release while working on the smaller updates and DLC. "For us to create future maps for Company of Heroes 3, we were going to have an issue that our assets were getting stale," Christie explains. So, as part of 3.0, Relic's art department created autumn and winter asset packs, as well as a new Industrial theme. This then created more work for the VFX team, who have added rain and snow, as well as a transition effect showing soil and concrete moving from dry to wet.

Not to be outdone, the design team also made significant changes to the singleplayer Italy campaign. The towns that dot the dynamic grand strategy-inspired map now have individual upgrades, making for more meaningful decisions when it comes to which settlement you capture next. And, responding to one of the main criticisms of Company of Heroes 3's singleplayer, they also updated the computer's AI so it makes smarter decisions in both the turn-based and real-time battles. "We wanted to get this feel like there was that sort of back and forth of the AI resisting you and pushing forward into your territory and actually taking your stuff, which wasn't really happening in any of the previous updates," Wrobel says.

Further complicating matters was the fact that alongside these regular updates, the DLC, and the big 3.0 update release work, was that Relic also released Final Stand in July, a roguelike horde mode spinoff of Company of Heroes 3. "We had to be very careful not to accidentally introduce this 3.0 work that was also happening at the same time," Christie says." The improvements in this update have also rolled out for the spinoff, too.

Naturally, Relic aren't doing all this work purely out of the goodness of the hearts. The regular updates keep players engaged, Christie explains, and "hopefully bring back lapsed players who were frustrated by some of these things." It's something the team have already seen happen before, Wrobel explains. "We saw with the 2.0 update that we had a big spike of users and that was great, but because that improved the overall quality of the game, we saw each month we were selling more copies than we were before. People have been buying these games for years and years and years, so if we invest in this now we're going to see returns for quite a long time into the future as well."

"If we were starting to see that tail down then we probably would have made a very different decision to be honest, but that's not what we see," Christie adds.

The next release for Company of Heroes 3 is a singleplayer DLC, Operation Torch, due out on November 25th. (So, if you're keeping count, that was also in the works while the update, battlegroup DLC, and spinoff were all being made.) Until now, Relic's additions to the RTS have been focused on the multiplayer community, adding new units to be used online or in offline skirmishes. Operation Torch brings new scripted missions that trace a set of soldiers moving through North Africa.

After that, though, I ask if Relic plans to continue adding to Company of Heroes 3 or if they're ready to move onto a new project. "Well, it's both actually," CEO Justin Dowdeswell tells me. "We would love to continue with Company of Heroes 3 and not solely as a place for us to experiment. That's one of the advantages of being smaller, and being able to make decisions. We're not going to leave Company of Heroes 3. It's an and function. We are going to embark on the next thing."

So, it doesn't sound like Relic are taking anything off their plate…

#3919. PlayStation Has No GOTY Nominee at The Game Awards for First Time in 12 Years

For the first time in 12 years — since all the way back in 2014 — there is no Sony-published PlayStation title amongst The Game Awards' Game of the Year nominees.

In that time, Sony has won three Game of the Year awards at Geoff's annual show, making it the most successful publisher in the event's history.

But its over-a-decade streak of nominations will finally come to an end here in 2026, as none of its releases from this year have made the cut.

That includes God of War: Sons of Sparta, Marathon, MLB The Show 26, Saros, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and Marvel's Wolverine.

In particular, Saros and Marvel Tokon got really strong reviews, but given just how stacked this year's competition is, it's no real surprise to see these relatively niche titles be left in the cold.

At the start of the year, many would have probably predicted that Wolverine would be in the mix — but a lukewarm critical reception has ultimately sealed its fate.

Just to recap, this year's Game of the Year nominees are as follows:

Again, since 2015, there hasn't been a single year where a Sony-published title has been ignored. Here's a full list of Sony's nominees in that time:

I don't think anyone would deny that Sony and its PlayStation Studios have had an off year. While their output has actually been quite frequent, none of their latest releases have made a lasting impact in the way that many of the above titles did in their respective years.

Do you think any of Sony's 2026 PS5 games deserved to be nominated for Game of the Year? Claw something out in the comments section below.

#3918. "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's closure

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

There was gore in the original Resident Evil?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most people don't associate the original Resident Evil with being overly grisly, but a lot's changed in the 30 years since it released. These days, we've become desensitized by dismemberment as a technical showcase rather than something to be horrified by, making 1996's Resident Evil look downright cozy next to today's horror pantheon. And yet, it was apparently shocking enough 30 years ago that series creator Shinji Mikami worried it wouldn't be fit for sale until Sony stepped in with some clutch packaging additions.

Mikami appeared on a Japanese podcast (timestamp) last month to talk about Resident Evil's legacy amid its 30th anniversary, but his comments haven't been widely reported until this week when Twitter user Genki started spotlighting the highlights. In one such example, Mikami tells the interviewers that OG Resident Evil was considered so "grotesque" that Capcom feared it wouldn't be fit for sale. We can only go off machine translation here as there's no English transcription, but Mikami says it was Sony that stepped in and saved the day by adding stickers to Resident Evil's packaging warning potential buyers of the game's gory nature.

Resident Evil creator Shinji Mikami says they were worried that the original Resident Evil game would not be allowed to go on sale because it was too grotesque but Sony had a solution that saved them. He said they didn't know what to do but Sony said that if they put a sticker on the game warning about the grotesque scenes then it would be okay to be released. Shinji Mikami says that really saved them. https://t.co/zgXIPPCIGQNovember 16, 2026

Mikami would continue to make excessively bloody games even beyond his time at Capcom with The Evil Within 1 and 2 at Tango Gameworks, but it's unclear if his next game has anything to do with the survival horror genre. He said in the same interview that his new studio Unbound is on track to release its debut title in 2027, but previous comments indicate he might be wanting to explore different genres after spending three decades scaring the bejesus out of players.

#3916. Nvidia shareholders have filed a lawsuit against the tech company over claims that they were misled regarding CEO Jensen Huang's affair

If I wasn't so sick of hearing about AI every day of my life at the moment I might have found it funny to hear that one of the biggest peddlers of the poison around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Oh who am I kidding, it is funny! And despite knowing that this won't likely push Nvidia away from AI, I am a bit tickled to hear that the tech company and Huang are on the receiving end of a lawsuit.

The suit in question, as reported by The Guardian, is based on a complaint filed in California's federal court on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher by Rosen Law Firm. Kistenmacher is an Nvidia shareholder, and with this suit he's seeking to "recover compensable damages," for himself and other shareholders due to the "precipitous decline in the market value of the Company’s securities." What a palaver! I do not imagine this will be resolved particularly quickly.

As it currently stands, Huang has only admitted to having an affair rather than any trade secrets being leaked anywhere. Nvidia had this to say on the matter: "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

The concern comes from the person Huang had an affair with, one Alice Huang (no, they aren't related), a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who have allegedly given Chinese companies Nvidia chips they bought billions of US dollars of. A messy situation to be sure, and one I unconfidently hope brings about the end of AI, somehow.

#3915. Marathon is becoming a whole new game next month with a roguelite PvE mode, a beta for a very Halo-esque team deathmatch mode, a vibey social space and more

Marathon is getting a lot bigger next month. In September, Bungie outlined their plans for the shooter making some big promises, namely the arrival of a PvE mode, and now they've shown off what you can expect from its next season, Symbiosis.

Top of the order is that PvE mode, which has a name now: Expedition. It's a roguelite mode, one that's playable in co-op, though a lack of details at this current time doesn't make it clear as to whether you can run it solo or not. The season's trailer, which you can have a gander at below, gives off the impression that you'll have to complete particular tasks before exfiltrating like you normally do. I'm sure we'll learn more in time.

The previously promised social space will be coming with this update too, and it's called Limbo. Morbidly appropriate! You can hang out here with your buds, head to a mini arena for some impromptu matches (I think), or head to the firing range where you can test out your weapons. You'll also be able to try out the new runner shell, Bishop, a cooler than you, samurai-sword-wielding robot who can jump real good and do that cool movie thing where it slices a whole bunch of enemies at once in one swing real quick like.

What will undoubtedly have some folks going "Halo's back!" is the beginning of a beta test for a team deathmatch mode. The Halo comparison is apt not simply because of the fact that it's Bungie who are making it, but because there's a deep-voiced announcer guy talking about all the sick kills you do. Details are slim on how this will work too. Beyond that, there's a few new weapons to flaunt, and maybe most excitingly, big ole alien enemies to take on.

You've still got a little while to wait for Symbiosis, which is currently slated to launch on December 8th. The game will be free to play from then until December 15th, too, obviously in a bid to show sceptics how good it is now (hopefully it is good, for Bungie's sake).

#3914. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

Wanda Maximoff's VisionQuest return proves why now is the perfect time for Scarlet Witch to take the limelight

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Avengers: Doomsday doesn't just mark Doctor Doom's arrival or the Avengers' return, seven long years after Endgame. It's easily the most ambitious endeavour Marvel Studios has ever undertaken, bringing MCU mainstays together with Marvel's First Family, the Fantastic Four, and Fox's original X-Men team.

Avengers: Doomsday is the culmination of storytelling that began at the turn of the century and that's obviously a very big deal, especially for superhero fans who have waited decades to see this epic team-up come to life on the big screen. Still, there's another, far bigger reason why people will be lining up for Doomsday on opening night, and her name is Wanda Maximoff.

Don't take my word for it. Disney reports that last week's VisionQuest finale helped "fuel a spike in ticket sales" for Doomsday while drawing in 3.7 million viewers on Disney+, a series high that represented a 44% jump from the previous episode.

The episode itself was decent enough, a fitting conclusion to Vision's journey, but it was clearly Wanda's return in a surprise post-credits scene that drove this sudden rush for tickets. Watching Doom reawaken Wanda and recruit her in his fight against the Avengers didn't just set up another plot point for Doomsday. It also confirmed that a fan-favourite character was finally set to return, four painstaking years after she appeared to die in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Vision star Paul Bettany explained in a recent interview how Marvel's head honcho dissuaded the VisionQuest team from bringing Wanda in sooner: "It will just fundamentally all become about WandaVision again," warned Kevin Feige – and he was right to say it. Although not even he could have predicted just how right he was.

Even though the Scarlet Witch didn't return in the main show, only popping up after the story had concluded, it quickly became clear from online responses that Wanda's return did in fact overshadow everything else that came before it (as it should). And that begs the question: If Wanda can generate so much buzz from just opening her eyes in a four-second cameo, imagine what she could accomplish with an entire movie of her own?

There's long been talk of a potential Scarlet Witch film, something which Elizabeth Olsen always seems keen for. Even after it seemed like Wanda might have died in the Doctor Strange sequel, Olsen assumed that this wasn't the end for her beloved character onscreen.

"I'm just making the assumption that they'll have me again," she told Variety in 2022. "I don't know to what capacity, but I hope I'm back. I hope there's also more fun to be had in something different. Where do we go? I feel like we've done so much with her. It's really been a wild couple years with her."

"Wild" is an understatement, not just for Olsen's experience of the character but for longtime fans who have suffered alongside Wanda over the years. Even before she arrived on screen, Marvel always did her dirty, like when they depicted her as a hysterical, unstable woman who erased all mutants in 2005's 'House of M' arc. It was also true again years later when the films followed suit, transforming the Scarlet Witch into a villain overcome with power and emotion.

WandaVision taught us grief is actually love persevering, and boy has our love for Wanda persevered through a lot. Still, it's easy to root for an underdog whose trials eventually shaped her into one of comicdom's most fascinating heroes. It wasn't until her solo turn in WandaVision, however, that all her flaws and complexity were brought to life onscreen, expanding her fanbase to the point where a solo Scarlet Witch film feels not just viable but necessary.

WandaVision taught us grief is actually love persevering, and boy has our love for Wanda persevered through a lot.

In an industry where female-led superhero films remain few and far between, it's about time Olsen was given the chance to spearhead her own movie. It's not like anyone was asking for four Thor films, yet it seems plenty of people are keen to see Wanda in theaters at this point, perhaps more than any other heroine these days.

But if we are going to do this, let's not rehash the crushing grief of WandaVision or the villainous tropes that we're leading into again with Avengers: Doomsday. Fans predict that Wanda's arc moving forward will likely echo the 2010's comic book storyline Children's Crusade where Doctor Doom took advantage of Wanda for his own gain before she was rescued by her kids and set on a path of redemption.

Given how VisionQuest just put the last pieces in place with the introduction of her now-adult son Tommy, it looks more and more likely that Wanda's story in Doomsday and Secret Wars will end with the entire Maximoff family reunited, which feels like the perfect starting off point for a Scarlet Witch movie.

Since her first full appearance in Avengers: Age of Ultron, MCU Wanda has been endlessly traumatised, losing her biological family first as a child and then her chosen family all over again in WandaVision. With so much build-up, a film led by Wanda could finally bring that full-circle, exploring what life looks like for her and the rest of the Maximoff family now that they're reunited at last, all working together as one.

The petition for WandaVision creator Jac Schaeffer to lead the project starts here. She was the one who devised their introduction as a unit in the MCU, centring the family dynamics which would be key to making a continuation of their story work on the big screen.

That, more than the threat they face, is what will be most important when it comes to pulling off a Scarlet Witch film… although the idea of pitting them against Aubrey Plaza's Death, last seen in Agatha All Along, is too enticing to ignore, especially as every member of that family has previously managed to evade her in some shape or form.

Connections to X-Men characters such as Magneto and Quicksilver, often depicted as Wanda's biological family in the comics, could also be explored now that Marvel's Merry Mutants are back on screen (although the MCU may wish to avoid over-complicating things in this fashion for now). Still, the possibilities are endless, which is fitting given that Wanda is a Nexus Being of infinite possibility.

Whatever happens, whether it takes a few years or a few decades, a Scarlet Witch movie feels inevitable at this point. Because why would Marvel refuse to print money? Sure, a film starring Wanda in the lead might have once felt improbable, but the Scarlet Witch has a knack for defying the odds, and there's never been a better time for her to take centre stage than now at the height of her powers, on and off screen.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives on December 16 in the UK and December 18 in the US. For more on the future of the MCU, here are all the upcoming Marvel movies and shows on the way.

#3912. Ahead of GTA 6 and as concerns over genAI PC ports grow, Take-Two's CEO says they're revving up their "technical defences" and "legal activites" over piracy

"[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that"

It's a bit of a time for AI and games at the moment, 'ey? A bad time, obviously, as it's infecting everything from game development, to the modding community, to native PC ports of a remake of a very popular game that I won't link to for fear of a certain company finding out where I live and ending me there and then. And of course, the latter may be a concern for one Rockstar Games and the impending release of GTA 6. But according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, game's publisher, they are currently technically and legally preparing themselves.

IGN recently spoke to Zelnick regarding potential AI cloning concerns, notably about any business issues they may face as a result. "I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business," Zelnick explained. "I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended."

Zelnick also made a comment about thinking "all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's," in response to a question about whether he wants to see OpenAI follow in Claude's footsteps by limiting the potential for genAI clones. "If you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected," he said.

It was during an investor Q&A where Zelnick dug into the precautions Take-Two are take-twoing in regards to the growing threat of AI. "[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Essentially: unless you want to face the wrath of the kinds of lawyers multi-billion dollar companies can afford, I wouldn't bother trying to clone GTA 6 with AI! Probably won't end well!

#3911. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

#3909. Ashes of the Singularity 2 review: Some neat ideas undermined by a rubbish campaign and obtrusive generative AI

Ashes of the Singularity 2 has some neat ideas for army management, but a poor campaign, an underwhelming new faction, and obtrusive generative AI use undermines the enterprise

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it? RTS sequel in the lineage of Supreme Commander

Reviewed On: AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Nvidia 2080 Super, 32 GB RAM, Windows 10.

Ashes of the Singularity 2 can't be faulted for scale. Much like its predecessor, the RTS sequel delivers on the promise of letting players control truly colossal armies. Rolling up huge globs of units and tossing them at your enemy lines in a giant, explosion-riddled mud fight is never subtle and only occasionally clever. But for any veteran RTS player, watching miles-long lines of armies clash is inevitably going to stir the soul.

Unfortunately, scale is also the sum of what Ashes of the Singularity 2 offers. As a sequel, it does little to build on the strengths of the original, while largely failing to address that first game's weaknesses. The campaign is terrible, the story borderline incomprehensible, and the whole experience is overshadowed by the spectre of generative AI.

Before we get into Ashes 2's numerous problems, I do want to give Oxide Games credit for one thing: for a game of this scale, Ashes of the Singularity 2 is remarkably easy to control. In terms of base-building, Ashes of the Singularity 2 is a largely familiar RTS affair. You build your production buildings, your resource harvesters, your defensive structures, and that's more or less it.

When it comes to unit recruitment, however, Ashes 2 is much more interesting. While units are still recruited individually, they're also automatically assigned into armies at the recruitment phase. You build a new army by queueing up all the units you want, and then when you're done, you assign a rally point for the army on the map, and all the units will just assemble there.

Once recruited, armies can be selected with the number keys and controlled like a single unit, and they tend to move and attack pretty intuitively, although pathfinding does struggle with narrow passes or rough terrain (which, to be fair are both things that real armies struggle with). This makes it very easy to oversee multiple armies at once.

In addition, when in battle, you can replenish destroyed units at the press of a button, or simply set the army to reinforce automatically. It's another convenient touch, and encourages you to support your forces by constructing new production buildings close to the frontline.

It's not the only area where Ashes 2 displays an intuitive flourish. Alongside selecting the relevant structure from the menu, you can also construct harvester buildings directly from the resource node, while upgradeable buildings will often display an upgrade button over them that you can click. In terms of UI/UX design, Ashes 2 successfully minimises rooting through menus. Everything is accessible through shortcuts, directly on the screen, or a single menu layer.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

This system does come at the cost of some finer control. Unit recruitment is bottlenecked to one unit per production building type, no matter how many buildings of that type you have. This means building an army composed of specific units (such as aerial units) takes longer, so armies tend to take a similar shape. On the subject of aerial units, they are a bit of a weak point for Ashes 2. Not only are they easily countered by AA units and emplacements, they also don't match the speed of ground units when in a mixed army, with a tendency to fly off and get themselves obliterated. Regardless, army control is by far the best thing about Ashes 2.

The sequel does introduce some other new features, such as a new faction, the United Earth Forces; unfortunately it's the least interesting faction in the game.

The UEF is a deeply vanilla sci-fi army, composed of tanks, jets and human soldiers so tiny they get instantly lost once the match scales up. It's way less compelling than the many mechs of the Post-Human Coalition, or the robotic insects of the AI Substrate. Where the Substrate's dreadnought units include a giant squid that fires laser beams and a blimp that shoots swarms, the UEF gets a big tank and a knockoff Megazord. Granted, the tank functions as a mobile base. That's useful, but it isn't fun.

The UEF is also the sole focus of Ashes 2's campaign. This is disappointing, but it's also the least of the campaign's problems. It's composed of 10 missions, roughly half of which are rigid tutorials with passive AI that offers virtually no challenge whatsoever.

The second half, which takes place in locations across the solar system, is better. The missions actually play with Ashes 2's scale and gradually let the AI off the leash. Indeed, the final two missions offer some pretty fierce resistance. But despite being set in locations like the Moon and on a weaponised asteroid bound for earth, they're also unambitious, meat and potatoes scenarios with no real twists or turns.

The result is four, maybe five hours of half-decent campaigning, which just isn't good enough in 2026.

The result is four, maybe five hours of half-decent campaigning, which just isn't good enough in 2026. It highlights how generous and meticulous Tempest Rising's campaigns were, built around thrilling, rapidly changing scenarios that sought to stretch the player's skills.

It doesn't help that the story is dreadful—a three way philosophy and ethics lecture between humans, AI, and uploaded post-human personality constructs. It's a parade of characters you never actually see babbling endlessly about the vague machinations of AI threats and whether or not post-humans are still the same people they were when they were bags of flesh and juice.

Ironically, the story is also where Oxide's use of generative AI is most evident. According to Ashes 2's Steam AI disclosure, Oxide used AI to "provide post processing effects and animation to art created by human Stardock artists for some of the campaign cutscenes" while "some cutscenes use Stardock human artist-made 3D assets with AI to composite the final shot." Finally, "some in-game unit barks, notifications, and a few minor characters use pre-generated ElevenLabs stock voices".

Frankly, I'm skeptical that this represents the limit of Oxide's AI use. All the character portraits look straight up AI generated to me, and the voice lines sound similarly infected. AI or not, it's something of a moot point because, either way, they're both awful. The portraits have that horrible, plasticky AI sheen to them, while the acting is often weirdly intoned in a way that does not help the narrative's bamboozling quality.

What bugs me most about Ashes 2's AI use, though, is that the RTS genre has such a rich heritage in cinematic storytelling. Warcraft 3, StarCraft 2 and Homeworld all successfully balanced their sci-fi grandeur with intimately human tales. Command & Conquer, meanwhile, was one of the earliest PC games to directly put a human face on videogame storytelling. From Kane to Tanya to Tim Curry escaping to the one place that hasn't been corrupted by capitalism, C&C's FMVs are often the thing that players most fondly remember.

I understand that Oxide Games probably doesn't have a Tim Curry budget. But it also doesn't need it. C&C's FMVs aren't remembered because they're expensive, or even especially great storytelling. They're remembered because they're fun, silly, intensely human creations. You don't need a massive budget to replicate that. If Oxide Games stuck a beret on a programmer and had them ham it up in front of the camera, the result would be infinitely preferable to Ashes 2's airy, inhuman waffle.

With the campaign a write-off, you're left with multiplayer and skirmish mode. Skirmish is arguably where Ashes of the Singularity has always been at its strongest, and playing against the AI here is certainly better than the campaign, offering a wide range of difficulty levels that lets you find your own sweet-spot. Putting together a four-way grudge match, watching the scale of the conflict slowly build-out, commanding multiple armies on multiple fronts, you get a sense of what Ashes 2 could be.

Yet here too, there are problems. None of the maps particularly spark joy. It's a roster of generic biomes and moonscapes that offer little in the way of personality or artistic direction. Also—and this is a broader complaint—while I appreciate that Ashes 2 is meant to be a slow-burn affair, I think it is a little too slow overall. In particular, battles are too attrition-heavy, and beneath the visual fireworks, you don't necessarily feel the punch of your units in combat. When Dreadnought units clash, it should feel like two gods have descended from the heavens. Instead, it feels more like two giant snails squabbling over a particularly large leaf.

It's a shame, because the work Oxide has done to make such an unwieldy concept so, well, wieldy is impressive. Given more care and time (and less generative AI), I think this could have been a great RTS. But with the campaign such a bust, what you're paying for here is one new faction, a skirmish mode and multiplayer, and after 10 years, I just don't think that's sufficient for a sequel.

#3908. Sony have cancelled Fairgame$, once again reminding us that chasing live service big bucks basically never works

You know, I'm sure that Sony had every intention of following through on their intention to release 10 live service games by 2026, as they mentioned way back in 2022. Well, as far as an intention that's designed to please shareholders can go, anyway. And now here we are, almost five years on from that comment that continues to haunt them with the news Fairgame$ has been cancelled.

This comes from a report from Bloomberg, who shared that, thankfully, there are no planned job cuts due to the game being cancelled. In a statement, Sony said that, "The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities, though didn't go into detail as to who those other teams are.

Bloomberg were also privy to a note shared with developers at Haven Studios from executives Sean Decker and John Doyle that follows a recent test of the game: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Sony have, notably, failed to capitalise on the live service trend; I'm sure I don't need to remind you about Concord. Hell, this isn't even taking the end of Destiny 2 into consideration, once a driving force of live service games, or how Marathon has struggled to pick up an audience in the way that Sony may want it to. You just can't force a game to be popular, especially in a genre like shooters.

For those that either missed or forgot about Fairgame$, it was announced back in 2023 and was supposed to be a "competitive modern heist game where you team up to break into exotic locations and steal the cargo," all while taking on security and other, real people. Gameplay was never formally revealed, only a CGI trailer, and was set to come to PC as well as PlayStation. Bloomberg also noted that the game had been reworked multiple times since the announcement and was set to be re-revealed with a new name. Ultimately, it looks like Katharine was a little generous with her timeline of six months.

"Can we share this memory and have it working 100% of the time"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI CEO and co-founder Sam Altman remains perturbed by discussion of his comments regarding RAM allocation prioritizing data centers over personal PCs, reiterating that everyone should "be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer" even if it is suboptimal.

Altman discussed the RAM market in a talk with Semafor (thanks, PC Gamer), returning to the well of controversy over his previous comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast.

Previously, Altman said, "From a global allocation perspective, actually it's quite terrible to have everyone have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and be used 5% of the time." Better, it would seem, to have that RAM always ramming in a data center.

As the collective internet began sharpening sticks, Altman corrected himself on social media, saying, "I actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers." (In the interim, one engineer made a tool that emails Altman about the unused RAM in your PC.)

This is the stance Altman takes with Semafor. "I want people to have a lot of RAM," he says. "I think everybody should buy a lot of RAM, be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer. I think this is good. I think the home tinkering is great."

Again, Altman says his original comment was "misinterpreted," even if "there is a true part of it." His defense of that part sees him repeat and expand on the argument that sparked this discourse to begin with.

"If we're going to be in this memory supply shortage," he continues, "then in some sense, whether or not we'll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference, the optimal thing would be: can we share this memory and have it working 100% of the time rather than sometimes off in someone's edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply maybe is not the reason to make the decision, but that's what I was trying to say."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

You might argue that this is the kind of conclusion you reach, and can only reach, by spending so much time with your head in the AI bucket that you forget to come up for air. Sure, reducing all recreational demand to an obstacle to efficiency and pondering a perfect world where even private machines are seemingly contributing to AI's march might sound out of touch, but at least Altman agrees "the home tinkering is great." Just one problem, as he notes: RAM prices have jumped "like 5x, 7x, something like that" in the wake of an industry that sold tickets to an arena it hasn't built.

#3906. Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3905. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

World of Warcraft: Forever's having some teething issues with its new spellcaster itemisation. The idea, to sum it up quick, is that a lot of the power that was in spells innately has been pushed onto items, instead, with the intention to make it feel really good when you get a cool new staff as a mage, for instance.

This has had unintended consequences, as discovered by Rextroy (the same madlad who solos raid bosses), as shared on YouTube. The problem is this: Gear in Forever can give a lot of raw power to your healing and damage spells, as part of the aforementioned changes. But that raw power also applies to lower-level healing spells, too.

In Forever (and in Classic), casting lower-level spells is a core part of managing your mana as a healer. In this instance, however, "the healing coefficient on healing power remains the same, which is around 43% [on a low level Flash of Light], so if I stack all healing green items, I get my healing power up towards 242," Rextroy explains.

This, combined with the Paladin talent Oath of Light (which slaps another 61 healing onto Flash of Light), along with Spiritual Focus and Concentration Aura, which makes it almost impossible for enemies to interrupt or push-back the casting of his Flash of Light, and this makes his paladin basically unkillable.

The low-rank version of his Flash of Light spell doesn't cost enough mana to outpace his natural mana regeneration, it heals for a bunch because of his gear, and enemies can't slow or interrupt it. Which makes him almost unkillable.

I say almost, because as his experimentations prove, he can still become stunned or crowd-controlled by high-level enemies. And there are limitations. While he can stand up to a level 60 enemy whacking on him, add two or three to the mix and he can no longer outpace their damage.

However, Rextroy finds a level 60 enemy he can kill, an abomination in Eastern Plaguelands, which he pulls using a bug that casts Echoes of Lordaeron, an anti-undead damage boost given to whichever faction controls the most towers in the zone, on enemies when he resurrects.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And sure, it takes 20 minutes. And sure, he can only kill it because the abomination has almost zero surprises, extra attacks, or abilities to stun him. But he still does it, getting a whopping… uh, 468 experience points for his trouble.

Perhaps the more game-breaking result of this build, then, is the fact that he can use it to out-pace fatigue damage, which generally stops players from swimming way out into the ocean. This lets him access a non-instanced version of the Drowned City dungeon, which is visible off the coast of Stranglethorn but cannot be visited outside of the dungeon without sleeping with the fishes.

While I think the extent of this build is probably something that'll get adjusted or patched out, I do sort of hope the spirit of it is kept the same—part of the promise of Forever was that weird item combinations or cool builds would emerge out of the woodwork and let folks do niche, but powerful things.

Perhaps it's not great that Rextroy can both tank and heal a dungeon with this setup at the same time, but I'd still like it to work in some capacity.

#3903. GTA 6 Nominated for Game of the Year Before PS5 Reviews Are Released

We got GTA 6 nominated for Game of the Year at The Game Awards before GTA 6.

The Game Awards 2026 has just announced the nominees across all its categories, and sticking out like a sore thumb is GTA 6.

It's the odd one out, because it's the only game shortlisted that has yet to release. Despite the fact it isn't out yet — and even that reviews have yet to land — Rockstar's hotly anticipated game is nominated across numerous categories.

In fact, it's the most-nominated game at this year's awards, with a total of eight nods if you include Manni L. Perez's nomination for Best Performance. It's up for the following trophies:

Yes, on top of all its other nominations, GTA 6 is in contention for Game of the Year.

There has been much debate online about whether the game would be considered for The Game Awards at all, given how close its launch is to the event itself.

Many believed it would not receive any nominations, because the nominee announcement was set to occur before GTA 6 launches.

However, the voting jury — which comprises hundreds of gaming media outlets from around the world — has deemed the game worthy of recognition in eight categories, more than any other 2026 title.

What's clear is that many jury members must have played the game, but more interesting is that they clearly hold it in high regard if it's been shortlisted for so many awards.

This has been quite revealing, then; it's a big hint at what critics think of the game, and we now also know (officially) who is playing the role of Lucia Caminos, one of the two lead characters.

#3902. Keeping hold of Company of Heroes was essential for Relic to leave Sega, Relic CEO says – "Without it we would have been a dead studio"

In the nearly 30 years since they opened their doors, Relic have been an enormously influential studio. Responsible for lauded RTS series Homeworld, Dawn of War, and Company of Heroes, they also dabbled in other genres with third-person shooter The Outfit and the original Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Yet, despite this history, in 2024, when Relic were negotiating their sale from Sega to UK investment firm Emona Capita, CEO Justin Dowdeswell knew the rights to Company of Heroes had to be part of the deal. "Without it we would have been a dead studio," he tells me.

Without naming names Dowdeswell points out that there are "numerous examples" of studios that weren't able to survive on their name alone. Not only did Relic need the ability to make more games in the series that they were known for, but they also needed the income from back catalogue sales a series like Company of Heroes provides.

Dowdeswell joined Relic shortly after Sega acquired the studio in 2013. This was in the immediate aftermath of publisher THQ's bankruptcy auction, where studios and franchises were sold off to the highest bidder. While Sega bought the studio, they didn't buy the licenses to everything Relic had created. "The other games that Relic made – Homeworld, Impossible Creatures, The Outfit... formative games in many people's memory – they were all split up, scattered," Dowdeswell says. "I think that was... I won't say a tragedy, but it's unfortunate because Relic is the home of those games. It would have been great for them to stay with the studio."

Just as a hint of the messy history of acquisitions and auctions: this year we see Dawn of War 4 coming from studio King Art Games and published by Deep Silver. Deep Silver are a subdivision of Plaion, formerly called Koch Media, which was acquired by Embracer Group back when they were called THQ Nordic. Not that they were actually the THQ that originally published Relic's Dawn of War, Nordic Games renamed themselves THQ Nordic after they bought the THQ trademark at auction.

As for Homeworld, Borderlands developer Gearbox picked up the license to the sci-fi RTS in the bankruptcy auction, then contracted Blackbird Interactive's support on the remasters, before handing the latter lead development on Homeworld 3. That chain of events does have a more clear throughline to Relic's past however, as Blackbird was created by two of Relic's co-founders Rob Cunningham and Jon Aaron Kambeitz. (Speaking of studios struggling without the series they made their name with, Blackbird was on the verge of bankruptcy before Gearbox got in touch with the Homeworld work. So we very nearly existed in a world where they never got to make the brilliant Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak and Hardspace Shipbreaker.)

None of this is intended to be a knock on Dawn of War 4. From what I've played it's a very good Warhammer 40K RTS, if it perhaps sticks a little closely to the model laid down by Relic's original. What do I know, though, talking about their own games, Dowdeswell tells me that while "one of the messages to the studio is we can't just make [the same] things that we made 20 years ago and hope it goes well", re-releasing the 20-year-old Dawn of War sold very well for Relic and netted the team some very positive reviews on Steam. "There's a bit of a paradox there," he adds"

Anyway, this is all getting side-tracked. Back to holding onto Company of Heroes when separating from Sega. "Fighting for Company of Heroes when leaving Sega was crucial because I already lamented the fact that the other games didn't come with Relic," Dowdeswell says. "I couldn't really imagine a Relic where none of the games that the studio has made and was known for were any longer part of it."

Relic and new owner UK investment firm Emona Capital LLP were able to negotiate Company of Heroes as part of the sale from Sega and since then the studio has spent the past two years focusing largely on supporting the WW2 RTS and restoring their back catalogue. The most recent update is the massive 3.0 patch to mark the series' 20th anniversary. Which, among many changes, overhauls the Mediterranean-set RTS game's special effects, audio systems, NPC AI, and makes significant changes to the singleplayer grand strategy-inspired Italy campaign, as well as adding a whole set of autumn and winter-themed assets for community map makers. They've also released a series of DLCs adding new factions to Company of Heroes 3's skirmishes and multiplayer, re-released Dawn of War with a definitive edition and announced they're doing the same for the original Company of Heroes, along with Blackbird Interactive's help. Dowdeswell says foundation building masks a lot of the work going on behind the scenes: "We now self-publish all of this," he explains. "There were a number of things that we had to learn, skills we had to develop, capacity and capability that we had to build at the studio very, very quickly."

I ask if it was always the plan to focus on their back catalogue, or if they had plans to release new games. Dowdeswell says spending four years quietly working on a new game wasn't an option: "It's almost impossible to do it that way because of the current climate in the industry. We don't have a financial safety net." Though, the team do have larger ambitions. "We want to make new games, we want to provide a modern Relic game," Dowdeswell says. "That ambition to re-establish Relic as an innovator in this strategy space is a big part of what drives our creative direction on new games." Focusing on updating Company of Heroes 3, releasing DLC for the game, and making definitive editions of Dawn of War and the original Company of Heroes is what gets the studio to the place it can make a new game.

However, Dowdeswell resists any framing of Relic's work on Company of Heroes 3 as spinning their wheels or resting on their laurels while working toward a new game. He argues the game "sits in between" Relic's past and its future: "It's an established game that came out three years ago, but it's also a way for us to take some chances, experiment a little bit, and while doing that staying really closely connected to the players, That's what the idea was behind the updates because it was a way to have very quick iterations and touch points with players and provide, honestly, a way for us to fund everything in the future."

As to what Relic is making next, Dowdeswell wouldn't say. Though, he revealed trying genres besides real-time strategy was "almost a certainty", before adding "I don't think it's going to be a vast departure for where we are, so it will still be strategic gameplay. We're not going to go build a racer."

Valve CEO and co-founder Gabe Newell has been under fire lately, pretty much entirely from Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, but the self-described "father of Lovecraftian gaming" has leapt to his defense. Without Newell, argues Doom and Quake veteran Sandy Petersen, PC gamers would have nothing to protect them from storefronts run by mega corporations.

"I know Gabe Newell. We have chatted at some length. I know numerous men who worked for him as well," writes Petersen on Twitter. "I am sure that there must be some disgruntled ex-employees out there but everyone I know who has dealt with him respects and admires him.

"And with Steam he is literally guarding the gates of Hell - preserving all gamers from the horrors of what would happen if parasites like Disney, EA, or MicroSoft became the providers ... May he live forever."

I know Gabe Newell. We have chatted at some length. I know numerous men who worked for him as well. I am sure that there must be some disgruntled ex-employees out there but everyone I know who has dealt with him respects and admires him. And with Steam he is literally guarding the gates of Hell - preserving all gamers from the horrors of what would happen if parasites like Disney, EA, or MicroSoft became the providers. May he live forever.November 16, 2026

Of course, Valve itself is a big corporation, but not nearly on the same level as Microsoft, Disney, or EA, and it's also a historically consumer-friendly one compared to other tech giants. Since I mentioned Sweeney, I'll use the example of Steam's mandatory AI disclosure, which requires developers to inform Steam users if there's any AI-generated content in their games. Sweeney has repeatedly railed against this in his full-throated embrace of AI in games, but Valve has shown no indication that it's considering walking back that policy even after a Steam Next Fest that was overrun by AI-generated games. Valve is far from perfect, but if you're gonna have one company all-but monopolizing the PC market, you could do far worse.

Petersen isn't the only one vouching for Newell. A recent video tour of Newell's ridiculous yacht, the Leviathan, revealed an endearing fact about the famously eccentric billionaire: he actually hangs out and eats with the crew on-board the vessel, proving that not every rich person treats regular people like insects.

Valve "played capitalism so well they broke it" and now Steam can never be replaced, former Epic dev says: "I don't think this is fixable"
