#3877. Review: GTA 6 (PS5) - The Greatest Open World Game Ever Made

What does eight years and an estimated $1 billion get you? Well, GTA 6.

In this long-anticipated crime sandbox, Rockstar has assembled the most technologically accomplished open world ever made, expanding on its groundbreaking work with Red Dead Redemption 2.

But crucially, with its dual protagonists Jason and Lucia, it’s grown up a bit.

This is the franchise at its most mature, shedding the cartoonish cultural caricatures of GTA 5 without losing the biting social commentary the series is known for.

The fictional state of Leonida is undoubtedly the star here; a dense and gigantic urban sandbox populated by an unfathomable array of art assets.

Whether it’s the easy-living coastal island of Key Lento or the mean streets of Crosstown, Rockstar’s artistry is utterly unprecedented.

Zoom in and you’ll see insects attracted to discarded food wrappers; a single convenience store has more unique art assets than entire districts in other open world games. This is remarkable stuff, delivered at such a scale it’s going to leave other publishers with their heads in their hands.

It feels alive, too; a casual visit to a gas station saw me berated by a cyclist for my wayward driving (I told him to chill out), while a brief pause on the side-walk ended up with my car getting hijacked by a masked criminal.

In over 150 hours of play, I’m still discovering random events that add depth and character to the open world. And even when the scripting is pushed to the background, the way every NPC feels designed, with distinctive personality and unique body types, makes this package an unfathomable feat.

But while Leonida is the standout, Jason and Lucia are the vehicles that guide you through it.

Just like GTA 5, each character has their own individual life, but the game is at its best when it brings them together.

I’ve never seen romance made into a mechanic quite like this, aside from perhaps the handholding in ICO, which is repurposed here. (Complete with DualSense haptic feedback when the characters touch.)

Jason is a bit of a beige blank slate, but Lucia brings genuine “girl power” to the story without pandering or feeling insincere.

In fact, in contrast to past GTAs, the many women in this instalment feel much more believable; the game frequently flips expectations on their head, without it ever coming across as forced.

A secret twist revealed in the opening moments adds gravity to the couple’s situation and becomes the driving force behind the story, which takes the pair from pillar to post, fulfilling the whims of a ragtag roster of ne’er-do-wells.

The campaign does fall into cliche territory at times, as the pair bounce from one bad idea to another in order to fulfil their ultimate ambition, and it’s something the characters seem to acknowledge. (“When are we going to get to call our own shots?” Jason wearily ponders at one point.)

But the mission design remains inventive throughout, regularly adding bespoke mechanics and interactions to keep things fresh.

In one early mission, Jason indulges his inner-PowerWash Simulator, as he rinses down a boat while other characters commentate key plot points. I won’t spoil the best moments, but needless to say there are missions here that will be remembered for a long time.

There’s also a slate of optional pastimes running concurrently to the main campaign which add genuine variety to the sandbox.

I was most enamoured by Jason’s home entertainment setup, which includes a distinctly PS4 coded console that can be powered up. I’ll leave you to discover his selection of fully playable games.

But beyond that, the ability to go hunting or even play a round of golf means you can lose yourself in this sandbox for hours at a time, and never really tire of the activities available to you.

Some of the action sequences remind me of all-time classics like Uncharted 3 – fist-pumping, set-piece heavy rollercoaster rides that push Rockstar’s engine to its limits, all within the confines of a meticulously designed open world.

Controller response is vastly superior to the studio’s previous games, with the cover shooting system feeling much more natural and the aiming mechanics buoyed by a pretty fun “bullet time” mechanic.

However, the game does fall into the trap of introducing heavily armoured bullet sponge enemies towards its conclusion, as it runs out of ways to make human-on-human encounters interesting.

That said, I really appreciated the agency GTA 6 gives you over how you approach each situation; non-vitals can be targeted to incapacitate enemies without murdering them, while it’s perfectly possible to sneak in and out of many areas without ever being detected.

This all builds a criminal profile which changes how the police and wider world will interact with you. Meanwhile, you can influence Jason and Lucia’s relationship itself, opting to keep them close or distant depending on how you want things to play out.

An early optional objective allows you to decorate Jason’s idyllic beach house in anticipation of Lucia’s arrival. Complete it in time and the couple will grow closer; ignore it and she’ll acknowledge you didn’t go the extra mile.

Other interactions are subtler: a kiss and cuddle on the balcony of the pair’s Vice City penthouse will strengthen their bond, but it’s up to you whether you want to invest in their relationship or not.

Multiple endings mean there are actual consequences to your actions, even if some decisions along the way feel more like an illusion than something truly meaningful.

The plot does begin to drag in its latter phases, and I do think Rockstar could have tightened up the roughly 60 hour storyline, which will likely take the average player around 80 hours to complete when accounting for the vast amount of side content as well.

(A 100% save could take anywhere up to 300 hours or more, depending on how much support you get from guides.)

As a crime sandbox, I also wanted to mention the ‘Wanted’ system, which has come on leaps and bounds.

A coordinated robbery can be accomplished without ever triggering a traditional car chase, as the game accounts for your outfit, vehicle, weapons, and much more.

Successfully scouting out your targets, and planning accordingly with a change of clothes and getaway car, can see you slip past the police undetected. Few moments in gaming are more satisfying than when you casually drive past a fleet of incoming cop cars, with a bag of successfully looted narcotics in your trunk.

Some players may respond negatively to the life sim elements here, which reward you for exercising and require you to occasionally put gas in your car or eat something.

But I think it adds to the immersive nature of the open world, and concessions have been made to the realism when it makes sense; a quick request to Scooter Bros, for example, will see your favourite car instantaneously delivered to your current location, so you don’t have to wait around.

The biggest downside to the outright awesome spectacle of the open world is that it runs at 30fps on the PS5 Pro, with no option to double the frame rate or tailor the presentation to taste, as has become standard in most other games.

Objectively this is disappointing, but given the sheer scale of Leonida I think it’s a necessary compromise.

It should be noted that despite all this, the frame pacing is solid and the game feels smooth and responsive as a result. I encountered very few (if any) instances of slowdown – even when flying over the map in a jet or speeding down highways being chased by rival gangs.

The audio presentation matches the high standards of the visuals, with different engine growls depending on how you’ve modified your vehicle. (Midnight Club fans may be excited to learn the racing missions here rival most dedicated franchises like Need for Speed alone.)

There are multiple fist-pumping audio cues, which leverage the title’s enormous licensed soundtrack to excellent effect. But credit must also go to composer duo Justice, who bring their distinct brand of disco-inspired electronica to the soundscape, elevating some of the best missions to impressive highs.

And I was blown away by how much texture the DualSense adds, with one of my favourite features being the feedback you feel when you pass cars at speed on the highway. The only thing I didn’t like was the use of adaptive triggers, which feel far too stiff and lack the nuance of first-party games.

GTA 6 is the deepest, densest, most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2.

Rockstar has set a new sandbox standard here, with a world that feels alive and populated with real people; Leonida is a place where it appears almost anything can happen at any time.

Crucially, despite the 30fps cap, the gameplay feels responsive and you have much more authorship over how you want to approach it. I enjoyed preparing for my robberies and feeling like I was rewarded for the legwork.

The audiovisual presentation is a new high for the industry, with a frankly flabbergasting array of art assets bringing it all to life.

But I think Jason and Lucia’s ragtag romance, which is central to everything in the game, also demonstrates an unexpected maturity – without completely removing the silly sense of downright dumb humour the series is known for.

Despite unprecedented expectations, GTA 6 delivers – and then some.

#3876. After being laid off by Microsoft, former Doom devs found new Smash TV-influenced FPS studio that isn't "subject to investor demands"

Their first project: televised deathgame shooter Danger Pay

Back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting. Now, a few of those devs have founded a new employee-owned studio, Hidden Horses. Their first project is Danger Pay, a single-player FPS influenced by ancient arcade blaster Smash TV (pictured) and dystopian movies such as deadly gameshow fable The Running Man – itself an influence on Smash TV.

Hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek. They're looking to make "the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of," in Land's words.

All members of Hidden Horses own a share of the company, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ. "Our structure is quite flat, and we elect leaders when needed," Willis told Vertical Slice in a separate interview. "Financially, this means we are not subject to investor demands and the preservation of the company and the jobs it sustains is paramount over needless growth and our 'capital' doesn't compete for returns with other potential investments."

All of which is obviously gesturing towards the horse elephant in the room: Microsoft, who've made enormous cuts to their Xbox biz in their eagerness to further supercharge their $4 trillion market value.

"We've replicated some things, changed some things, and added others [from our id Software days]," Willis went on. "Overall, I think top-down hierarchy is something we all have bad experiences with—we also don't want to trend chase or make a game by focus group. We want to make the kinds of classic gameplay focused games that we would play ourselves. We think there is a market for that and our experiences with the gaming community in our past work history informs that."

Willis's hope is that the "flat" structure will motivate staff to work harder, because they feel like they have a meaningful say over the company's direction. "It allows all ideas to be considered and means we don't miss out on any contributions from our employees just because they don't sit high up in some arbitrary hierarchy," he said..

I'm cynical about "flat" company structures, myself. I think they are very often just an excuse for the biggest egos in a company to throw their weight around. It can work given a friendly initial mix of founders, but it gets complicated when you start hiring new people who don't have the same chemistry. Mind you, there are no plans to expand the company dramatically for the foreseeable. "We want to create a vehicle that allows us to make games for our livelihoods, not to make crazy profits and get 100x returns," Willis went on. I'm also a bit leery of the fact that Hidden Horses have popped up a Kickstarter, because I'm leery about crowd-funding in general, even when Peter Molyneux isn't involved. The studio founders are currently working on some promotional initiatives to drum up support, including a studio documentary and *squints* a promotional beer? Still, I'm happy to hear that at least a few Cacodemon wranglers jettisoned by the big M have landed on their hooves feet. I wish Hidden Horses the best of luck with it all. As for Danger Pay, proper screens, footage and release details are to follow.

Avengers: Doomsday looks set to be the most violent Avengers movie yet. The film has been rated PG-13 for "violence/action, bloody images, and language", according to Film Ratings.

The detail of "bloody images" is new territory for the Avengers franchise. According to ComicBook.com, Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame were rated for "sci-fi violence" but this is the first time "bloody" has been used. The movie has not yet been rated in the UK, but this could give some more insight into how dark the MCU movie might go.

We know the stakes are high in Anthony and Joe Russo's return to the big screen with Doomsday as heroes from three universes are teaming up to face Doctor Doom. The Fox X-Men, the Fantastic Four, and the OG and new Avengers must all work together to deal with the threat.

However, it seems like Doom has been building his own team, recruiting Bruce Banner in the Avengers: Endgame Encore post-credits scene and resurrecting Wanda Maximoff in the VisionQuest post-credits. Given the news that the movie will feature "bloody images", we're almost certain that some big casualties are on the way.

Kevin Feige recently revealed they had been planning to bring Doom in for a long time, even pre-dating the exit of Jonathan Majors as Kang the Conqueror. In fact, he revealed they approached Robert Downey Jr.'s agent at the Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania premiere about the potential return.

However, despite sharing the same actor, the Marvel head confirmed that Doom is not a Tony Stark variant. "He's Victor Von Doom," he told Empire magazine.

We're now a month out from Doomsday as it arrives in UK cinemas on December 16 and US theaters on December 18. For more, check out our guides to upcoming Marvel movies and shows as well as our breakdown of the Marvel timeline.

#3874. "One of those ways where you can use AI ethically": CDPR have modified Geralt's Polish voice in The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past with genAI, due to actor's stroke

Jacek Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing

CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion. The move's been made with the permission of Geralt's Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, and is rooted in the studio wanting his new lines to sound similar to the ones he recorded for the original game prior to having a stroke which has altered how he sounds.

Game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen update, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted". With next year's Songs of the Past expansion, CD Projekt Red were seemingly more concerned about making sure lines recorded by post-stroke Rozenek don't sound markedly different to those he recorded a decade ago for the base game and its existing expansions.

After a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings. Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing for this to go ahead. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," he told Game File. "I have great trust...for the creators of this game."

This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red have enlisted Respeecher's services. Back in 2023, it was revealed that the studio had used speech synthesis software to make ripperdoc Viktor Vektor's lines in the Polish version of Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion sound like actor Miłogost Reczek. Reczek died in 2021 before he could reprise his role as Vektor for the DLC, so rather than recasting the character across the whole game to avoid noticeable differences in voice, CD Projekt got another actor to voice Vektor's new lines for Phantom Liberty, then used the genAI tech to make those lines sound like Reczek was delivering them. CD Projekt Red said at the time that they'd gotten permission from Reczek's family before going ahead with their plan.

Speaking to Game File about this latest use of genAI on Rozenek's Songs of the Past lines, CD Projekt localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed noted that "as a person working with voice actors over all the regions in the world, this is a big concern". "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," he added. The argument the studio are making at current is that this was "a special case" due to Rozenek's specific situation with Songs of the Past.

Geralt's English voice actor Doug Cockle reportedly won't have his lines for the new expansion get the same genAI treatment, nor will any lines Rozenek records for future Witcher games, with the studio seemingly happy to lean on the passage of in-game time as an explanation for Geralt sounding different in the latter case.

As ever, there's a debate to be had as to whether CD Projekt Red should have simply recast Rozenek's role in Songs of the Past if the difference bothered them so, possibly while bringing the actor on to help tutor whomever his human replacement for Songs of the Past would be in nailing the exact gravelly tone needed for Geralt. That way, you'd have two actors being paid for work rather than forking out for genAI instead of one of them, though it's possibly an idea that'd only work well in theory. If I were Rozenek I'm not sure I'd be totally happy aiding someone who could potentially be tapped to replace me going forwards, though it does very much seem like the lesser of two evils when compared to the potential of voice actors being replaced by genAI line readings.

As far as the game alone is concerned, I'm also not sure Geralt's voice being different in the new expansion is something that'd bother me too much when playing. One would assume he'd not suddenly be sounding like a member of Alvin and the Chipmunks, and there are plenty of storyline justifications you could concoct or lean on for him sounding that bit gruffer at times.

#3873. Rockstar details Grand Theft Auto 6 PS5 Pro enhancements, but it'll still only run at 30FPS

Pushing consoles to "their absolute limits".

As Grand Theft Auto 6 preloads go live, developer Rockstar has detailed the enhancements coming to the PS5 Pro version of the game, confirming these won't include framerates above the 30 FPS its targeting for consoles.

Rockstar shared the news in a blog post released to announce that GTA 6 pre-loading is now available ahead of its release date on 19th November.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles," Rockstar says. It goes on to reconfirm GTA 6 is targeting 30 FPS on all consoles, saying the game is pushing modern machines "to their absolute limits" in order to "bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

PS5 players can expect high-fidelity haptic feedback through the DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio, and Tempest 3D audio, while PS5 Pro enhancements come in the form of PSSR support and ray tracing shadows, which should make the game look especially fancy, plus improved load times. PlayStation players can also expect remote play support. As for the Xbox, the post clarified details on Xbox Cloud Gaming, which will allow the game to be streamed to Xbox consoles including the Xbox One. Notably, this won't work on PC.

Grand Theft Auto 6's 30 FPS target was previously confirmed by Rockstar back in August, but there was some uncertainty around a possible 60fps performance mode at the time. Still, those PS5 technical boons do a lot of work to improve the games it's applied to, which if nothing else should mean GTA 6 will be quite the looker.

What do you mean bad actors I wasn’t doing that much bad things pic.twitter.com/swHfeOLTuVNovember 16, 2026

Bitly, the URL shortener website, got in hot water this week as users (or 'bad actors' as the company calls them) found out they could hijack old broken links and put whatever they like in their place. As you can imagine, chaos ensued.

Many of the links have since been fixed, but it seems like the McDonald's Twitter account once accidentally said the Swedish McDonald's team are responsible for 9/11,, and KFC linked to the Mewgenics wiki page for Steven, an NPC from the game. McDonald's was caught multiple times in this hijacking, with the Canadian X account hijacked to link the We Are Charlie Kirk song.

Though it's hard to verify now, it also seems like the Windows X page accidentally linked to the "r/FuckMicrosoft" subreddit too.

Big brands weren't the only ones caught in the mass hijacking. President Donald Trump seemingly tweeted a lot of Bitly links back in 2011, which were hijacked to instead link to a 'Trollface' meme song, a picture of a soggy cat titled "Soggy cat", and a link to the Epstein files Wikipedia page.

images for archival purposes pic.twitter.com/fRRr8LMGeENovember 15, 2026

A day after this exploit started to make its way around X, Bitly shared that it had identified the issue and said, "We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future."

It seems like the links in question were broken before being hijacked, and users simply managed to redirect those links to whatever site they wanted. However, in Bitly's documentation, it says the "back-halves used on these links cannot be re-used — whether they're automatically-generated or custom back-halves." So it's not entirely clear how these users manage to use links when Bitly says they supposedly cannot be reused.

Earlier today, we identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts. We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working…November 15, 2026

In the grand scheme, brands linking to various songs and Wikipedia articles are relatively harmless, but the ability to hijack links does pose a problem: what if hackers could do the same with a link to something containing malware? As such, it's probably a good reminder to Bitly and any other URL shortener websites to double-check that users can't reuse old broken links, as who knows who could have possibly made them first.

#3871. 'PS5 Pro Is Not Powerful Enough to Run GTA 6 at 60fps': Rockstar Explains Frame Rate Decision

I’ve played GTA 6 on PS5 Pro for over 150 hours and it’s a remarkable experience. You can read my review through here.

This is the densest open world ever designed. The sheer amount of art assets on screen at any given time is simply unprecedented.

There is a downside to all the detail, though: the Rockstar release bucks contemporary console trends and runs at 30fps, without compromise. There’s no Performance option, even on Sony’s most powerful platform, which will run you $900 these days.

I spoke to Rockstar’s Marc Chambers, the man in charge of Technology Production to try to understand why.

“The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the games visual fidelity,” he said.

“While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it’s not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”

In other words, it’s as many already predicted: GTA 6’s performance is limited by its robust CPU demands.

Chambers continued: “GTA 6 pushes the current-generation console hardware to its absolute limits. The complexity of simulating and rendering the environments and inhabitants in a world the scale of Leonida, while maintaining the density, visual fidelity, and player agency we envisaged, places extraordinary demands on the hardware. Bringing all of these systems together and completing the required work for every frame is only just possible within a ~33ms frame budget.”

The remarkable thing to me is, despite the drop to 30fps, I found the game to feel very responsive overall. Aiming is snappy and movement feels less cumbersome than in past Rockstar releases, like Red Dead Redemption 2.

Rockstar’s Vice President of Technology David Hynd told me that the team was able to remove one full frame of delay compared to past titles.

“The input controller is sampled as late as possible during the game update. As a consequence, the game is updated with the most recent input data and we minimise the time between pressing a button and seeing the results on screen,” he said.

You really do feel this: I was switching between GTA 6 and several other 60fps PS5 games during the review process, and while the frame rate difference was obvious to my eyes, it didn’t feel as dramatic as I’d expected.

“For our game mechanics, we ensured that we stripped as much ‘dead space’ out of the start of our animations as possible,” Hynd continued. “And ensured that we could seamlessly interrupt them as early as was practical.”

There are still moments where GTA 6 feels clumsy, but it’s a marked improvement in playability compared to past games, despite the drop in frame rate.

Overall, I think Rockstar made the right decision.

The decision to lock gameplay at 30fps is objectively disappointing, but on a PS5 Pro the performance is smooth throughout, and the controller response is surprisingly good.

With the sheer amount of art assets on the screen at any given time, I think it would have been a shame to see Rockstar compromise its vision.

This is the most immersive open world ever made, and I think it’s clear the team has put as much thought as possible into making sure it feels smooth and responsive at 30fps.

Review GTA 6 (PS5) - The Greatest Open World Game Ever Made

#3870. Grand Theft Auto 6 becomes the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation Store history

UPDATE: And the most pre-ordered game in Xbox Store history.

UPDATE 11TH NOVEMBER: Grand Theft Auto 6 has also become the most pre-ordered game "of all time" on the Xbox Store, Microsoft has announced. And on that platform, again, the advice is to pre-load because of "unprecedented demand" for the game, a post on Xbox Wire said.

The Xbox difference is that you can use Xbox Cloud to stream GTA 6 to other Xbox devices, although not PC, notably - the game isn't available on PC and presumably Rockstar doesn't want it playable there by any means. Microsoft's stream-deal with Rockstar has also expanded to include Red Dead Redemption 2 "and more", which will be available to stream in the "coming months".

ORIGINAL STORY 10TH NOVEMBER: Sony has just announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 has become "the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store". Note, it's not the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation history, just on its digital PlayStation Store.

The announcement, which comes as Sony prepares to ditch physical releases for an all-digital future, was made in a PlayStation Blog post confirming pre-loads for GTA 6 are now live.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store," Sony wrote. "Given this unprecedented demand, we've joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they're ready to play on launch day.

"We strongly advise that everyone who is hoping to play on launch day to pre-load the game as soon as possible," the blog post added. So: consider yourselves advised.

GTA 6 becomes available as soon as your region's clock ticks over from midnight into 19th November, which, if you're in New Zealand, means you'll play the game before everyone else. If only there were a way to pretend you lived there...

Elsewhere in the blog post, Sony underlined some features coming specially to GTA 6 on PS5 and PS5 Pro. On Xbox, meanwhile, cloud streaming is supported, but not - sadly - to PC.

Last night, in a Take-Two financial earnings call, company leader Strauss Zelnick said pre-orders for GTA 6 are tracking "far above expectations" and that soon, "numbers will speak for themselves". Presumably because they will be gripped by an excited form of sentience. It's expected that GTA 6 could become the best-selling instalment in an already mega-selling series; Zelnick reckons GTA 6 will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two in terms of success.

#3869. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

So, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

By way of example, one of the largest new AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to currently have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a new phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

In fact, Samsung and LG, the two big noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for new PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I said, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

What is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

Monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

Oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Anywho, one immediate and rather ironic issue is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

The bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

By way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for big-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

The 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a big-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

That's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the new Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

One could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

That said, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

Until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.

The leaker who broke the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has some not-so-good news about Majora's Mask.

Back in March of this year, known leaker NateTheHate broke the news that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake would be happening this year, alongside a new Star Fox, Switch Sports game, and Switch 2 Edition of Pikmin 4 – as well as no 3D Mario, which is apparently planned for 2027. NateTheHate correctly predicted the Switch 2 reveal date in 2025, but this string of correct info has made him a pretty trusted leaker within the Nintendo community. Which is why this news brings me no joy.

After The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's success, everyone is certain that a Majora's Mask remake has to be coming soon given the game follows up Ocarina's story as well as reuses a ton of assets from the game. In response to a Twitter user asking about the status of a Majora's Mask remake, NateTheHate responds, "Can only comment on Majora's Mask and it's that I've heard nothing to suggest any such project is currently active."

@tennek027 Can only comment on Majora's Mask & it's that I've heard nothing to suggest any such project is currently active.November 17, 2026

Of course, this is an apocalyptic blow to the level of the moon falling on Termina for those who somehow hoped Nintendo would pull a Capcom with Resident Evil 2 and 3 and release a Majora's Mask remake in a year's time.

That being said, I wouldn't lose too much hope. After the success of Ocarina of Time, the easiest win Nintendo could have is to work on a Majora's Mask remake. It happened on the 3DS, it can happen again.

Since 2013, The Legend of Zelda has pretty much been a yearly franchise, with 2022 being the only year since then we didn't get a new game, a remake/remaster, or a Hyrule Warriors game. It's pretty obvious that Nintendo wants to keep the series on people's minds constantly, and one of the easiest ways for Nintendo to keep things up is through remakes, which take a bit less effort than conceptualizing a new game.

I just hope Nintendo stays strong and doesn't listen to the contingent of people who want the timer removed from the game. As someone who saw the Dead Rising series turn into trash with its fourth entry as Capcom made the time mechanics less and less prevalent, and saw people trying to do the same to The Blood of Dawnwalker through modding, I've become a hardcore time limit defender.

#3867. Here's our second wave of PS Plus games for November 2026 - and Sony's scrapping its barely used PC app

Death Stranding 2! Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii! Atomfall!

Sony's revealed the second wave of games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra this month, and there are some genuine big-name attractions, led by Hideo Kojima's futuristic delivery man showstopper Death Stranding 2: On the Beach.

Here's the new games coming PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium in November:

And here are a couple of games coming only to PlayStation Plus Premium in November:

There's a lot to recommend in that list. Death Stranding 2 was one of the standout games of 2025. "A busier, louder, and more emotionally resplendent take on this singular hiking sim," Lewis Gordon wrote in Eurogamer's Death Stranding 2 review.

Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii also shone brightly last year, as ridiculous as it was. "A raucous, absurd spin-off that manages to still feel like a first-rate Yakuza game despite the leftfield setting and delightfully unhinged plot," wrote Matt Elliott in Eurogamer's Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii review.

Meanwhile, Atomfall - Rebellion's quirky British take on a Fallout-like post-apocalyptic idea - was awarded three out of five stars. "If you can get over a difficult start and fancy a lean take on the survival genre, Atomfall delivers an intriguing tale worth discovering," Tom Orry wrote in Eurogamer's Atomfall review. It's presumably been significantly patched and smoothed since then.

The Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake also scored three out of five stars. "Some excellent enhancements make this the ultimate version of Dragon Quest 3, but it could still do more to make it wholly welcoming to newcomers," Daniella Lucas wrote in Eurogamer's Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D review.

We didn't review Hell Let Loose, but the popular World War 2 shooter would go on to amass a serious following and spawn a follow-up game in Hell Let Loose: Vietnam recently, which we did review. "The lavish jungles, rigid command structure, and emphasis on communication make Hell Let Loose: Vietnam a fascinating war simulator when it works. But its many variables can all too easily devolve into a miserable snipe-fest," Rick Lane wrote.

There's plenty to be getting on with, then.

Sony also announced in the PlayStation Blog post it's retiring the PS Plus app on PC from 10th December. Why? Because nobody really uses it.

"With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4 percent) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use," Sony wrote. "As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available."

For more information on PlayStation Plus, you can check out our guide to PS Plus and all the available games here.

#3866. Nvidia board reportedly prepare to give CEO Jensen Huang the boot, as second alleged affair thrusts him closer to seriously lusty Crusader Kings playthrough territory

The next step's usually a desperately initiated sway scheme

The situation at the highest levels of AI and also some graphics cards if you insist company Nvidia continues to look, well, less than ideal. CEO Jensen Huang, he of the reported extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, now appears to potentially be on the verge of being chucked out of the window of a black and green corporate tower, following a report claiming that he had a second alleged affair with an executive who reports to him.

The New York Times report that Huang's second alleged extramarital affair was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, responsible for the company's tech being adopted in the medical field for the likes of imaging and aiding in drug discovery. If that's the case, at least this time there won't be any strongly-worded denials of espionage from the Chinese government, though it would still very much be an internal nightmare for Nvidia.

So, Huang has so far not caused more than one international incident with his alleged infidelity. Still, Nvidia's board are reportedly preparing to oust the CEO from his post. That's according to the Wall Street Journal, with other publications currently only going as far as reporting that the board are weighing up whether to give Huang the boot.

Earlier this week, Nvidia shareholders filed a lawsuit in California against the company over claims that they were misled regarding Huang's alleged affair with the suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia's shares have dipped following the reports of the alleged affairs.

With Huang potentially poised to go, chatter about possible successors has already kicked off. Elon Musk, meanwhile, has taken to the social media hellscape he owns to suggest he'd be up for hiring Huang if the exec is ousted from Nvidia. Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney is also on there calling for Huang's job to be saved, because of course he is.

The question all of this has left me with, aside from wondering why people in real world power insist on behaving like they've gotten a bit bored in the middle of a Crusader Kings 3 session, is this: is there someone on hand who can try to describe 63-year-old nerdy businessman Jensen Huang like he's some sort of irresistibly sexy heartthrob? "Huang isn't the usual CEO. He is a charismatic, leather-jacket-wearing apostle of Nvidia chips who built the company on processors for video games, transformed it into an artificial intelligence machine, and, in turn, created the most valuable company in the world."

I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Look, I'll be real with you. When I installed Drag Meets – Quick n Dirty Edition, I was not expecting it to go well. Cars spend most of their time flying and exploding in my copy of Grand Theft Auto 5, and these circumstances aren't conducive to gentlemanly racing.

I didn't anticipate it going quite as badly as it did, though. Drag Meets is actually rather complex: you don't just rock up to an objective marker, tap E, and get warped behind the wheel of a car. There's a lite social sim element to the whole thing, so you walk up to an objective marker, tap E, and suddenly find yourself standing in the midst of a drag racing soirée.

Drag meets are a scene, it turns out, and the scene's members have names, goals, and ambitions. A racer named "Blue Anime Panto" is seeking a challenger, the notifications inform me. "Blade had joined the meet", reads another. A lady called Tempesta has been forced to leave the meet because her engine broke, apparently. How did this happen? Either it's a randomly rolled event or her car flew into the sun; I am unable to tell.

It's not just Tempesta who's leaving the meet. Everyone is leaving, on account of the airborne minivan, just overhead, filled with hitmen determined to kill us all. They should be determined to kill me and only me, but Lamar (from GTA 5, you know? Lamar was also there. Keep up) began shooting back at them and all hell broke loose.

The drag race—if it's even possible—never got the opportunity to start. Pretty soon, racing legends like Stinger GT and Rhapsody were face-down in the Los Santos grass. And then I teleported to the airport.

#3864. Guide: Who Is the GTA 6 Cover Art Girl and Is She Based on a Real Person?

What we know about the GTA 6 cover art girl so far

GTA 6 is going live now worldwide, and that means you might have more questions about the cover girl on the box art. In this GTA 6 guide, we're covering who is the GTA 6 cover art girl and is she based on a real person?

On this page: Who Is the GTA 6 Cover Art Girl and Is She Based on a Real Person?

With GTA 6 now available, we'll be able to find out if the cover art girl actually appears in the game. Up until now, Rockstar hasn't commented on who she is.

At the time of writing, with the game going live worldwide, there hasn't been any evidence of the GTA 6 cover girl being found in the game.

GTA games have often had women on their box arts, but it's important to note this doesn't necessarily mean they'll play an important role in the story — or even appear at all. History has taught us the girls on the front cover can sometimes appear in minor roles within the plot, but they're usually not critical to the story.

For example, the cover girl from GTA 5, the girl taking a picture in a red bikini, doesn't appear in the game whatsoever. It is the same for GTA 4: the girl wearing a red top and licking a lollipop isn't in the game. In fact, in terms of the mainline entries, you'd need to go back to Vice City for an example of the cover girl actually being in the game.

As such, there's a chance the GTA 6 cover girl is purely for promotional purposes — she might not be in the game at all.

So, there's a fairly good chance the GTA 6 cover girl won't be in the game itself, but is she based on a real person? While developer Rockstar hasn't said yet, the Internet believes it's found someone with a very, very strong resemblance.

Gabriela Chiquin, who is an influencer, DJ, and musician from Venezuela, looks a lot like the GTA 6 cover girl. In a number of Instagram posts, she has her hair curled similarly to the cover girl, and wears green clothing. The pictures of her in green are from a few years ago, so they weren't taken in response to the attention she's gotten from the link to GTA 6.

Having caught wind of the similarities, she said in an Instagram post: "I want to thank the entire GTA community for so much love. I never imagined receiving so many messages, comments, and memes." She doesn't actually say whether she is the GTA 6 cover girl or not, however.

The cover girls for its game isn't something Rockstar usually makes a big deal out of, so it's unlikely we'll ever get official confirmation that Chiquin is the actual inspiration for the GTA 6 cover girl. Still, there's a very clear resemblance here, and the Internet managed to make the connection within days.

#3863. PlayStation's embattled shooter Fairgames has finally been cancelled, a new report says, as live service push withers away

After years of silence, we finally know the fate of PlayStation's embattled live service game Fairgames. The Haven-developed co-op heist shooter has been cancelled, with the silver lining that the studio is not closing down or laying off staff.

According to a new Bloomberg report, the decision to cancel Fairgames was made following the results of a recent playtest. Sony told staff on Tuesday of the playtest's poor reception and of its decision to end development.

"While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle reportedly wrote in an email to staff.

"Combined with challenging market conditions in the PvP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

A PlayStation spokesperson later confirmed that developers at Haven will now support other teams within the PlayStation Studios group, as they continue to "explore new creative opportunities".

Fairgames was initially announced in 2023 as one of several in-development live service games, as part of an initiative by former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan to create more than a dozen games that generate recurring revenue.

Most of those titles were cancelled before they were even revealed, and those that made it out, such as Concord, flopped severely. Even Sony darling Guerrilla Games seemingly can't make it work, with recent reports saying the studio's Horizon Hunters Gathering - initially envisioned as a live service spin on the robo dinosaur series - will now shift into a more traditional co-op structure without live service elements. That's assuming the team can show a revamped version of the game to executives by December.

The news of Fairgames' cancellation isn't surprising. The game has had a tumultuous development journey ever since its reveal. Initially set for release in 2025, the game was soon pushed back to 2026, following the departure of studio founder Jade Raymond.

Though Sony later reiterated its commitment to its remaining in-development live service titles, Fairgames was never shown to the public again. That same year, game director Daniel Drapeau left Haven - another key departure suggesting the game had difficulties and might not see release.

Throughout that time, Fairgames has reportedly been reworked multiple times, with a plan for it to be re-revealed under a new name. That name is believed to be Break In, linked to a trademark Sony filed in May, but with the project cancelled, we may never know if that was the case.

#3862. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang resigns amid scandal surrounding two alleged affairs, interim CEO appointed as search for sexy leather jacket man's successor begins

Guess his desperately initiated sway scheme failed, then.

Nvidia have ripped off the wax strip and are looking for a new CEO. Jensen Huang, he of the reported extramarital affairs with both a suspected Chinese spy and one of his executive underlings at Nvidia has removed his bottom from the great throne of black and green graphics cards.

"Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," Nvidia declared in a press release announcing the "CEO transition" they're embarking on. Stepping up to replace Huang for the immediate future is current Nvidia executive vice president and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who is becoming interim CEO on top of her established number-crunching duties.

One would assume she's quickly calculated just how much extra work Jensen's alleged inability to not get amorous with women who aren't his wife will add to her plate until a permanent successor is found. Speaking of that, Nvidia wrote that they "will consider internal and external candidates" in their scanning for someone to step into Huang's leather jacket. Actually, Nvidia folks, maybe don't let the new person wear the leather jacket, lest people potentially find them dangerously attractive. Failing that, maybe a pair of padlocked underpants are in order, adorned with flashing green lights to ensure brand recognition in trouserless scenarios.

The company's board of directors have gone ahead and appointed Harvey Jones as their first ever chairperson, one would assume to help convince money people that they've got strong enough leadership in place until their new permanent boss is found.

"Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," interim CEO Kress said "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Goodbye, leather jacket man who was allegedly too sexy for his own good, despite being a nerd who stands on stages waving hardware about. Odds are we'll see you again, possibly in the company of Elon Musk, because execs can never be allowed to be out of lucrative work for more than five minutes.

The Ghoul is still on the hunt for his family in Fallout, with actor Walton Goggins saying the ongoing search could change his character's outlook in the third season of the Prime Video series.

"If you never got to see a loved one, and you found out that those loved ones were still alive, what might you experience after not seeing them for a very long period of time, what would that mean to you?" Goggins pondered about the Ghoul's upcoming arc at an awards screening attended by GamesRadar+.

As a refresher, the Fallout season 2 ending saw the Ghoul uncovering at least part of the mystery of his missing wife and daughter – namely, that they were still alive. But they were since taken to Colorado for reasons unknown, with the Ghoul on their tail.

"So that's what we all spent the better part of this season really asking ourselves, and you know whether I discover them or whether I don't discover them in season three is really irrelevant to me," Goggins added.

Then, a line that cuts deep into the Ghoul's motivations for the upcoming season: "Well, then, what does that mean to you if you get what you've been looking for for 200 years? And how does that change you? What does that really mean to you?"

So, when might Fallout next drop on our screens? Recently, we had a bombshell courtesy of Hank actor Kyle MacLachlan, who told a fan that the third season could drop in May or June of next year.

Beyond that, who knows? Goggins himself doesn't have the intel on a fourth season, and a recent Instagram post from the actor sounded more like a goodbye to the show than we were expecting.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has been a huge success for Nintendo, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game ever, shifting more than 5.2 million copies in four days.

Nintendo announced the sales result this morning in a press release, specifying that the record relates only to Nintendo-published games. But since Nintendo's games are the most popular Switch 2 games, the fastest-selling-ever title presumably holds.

It's an incredible result for a game that's been received with enormous enthusiasm. This level of success begs the question of whether Nintendo would consider remaking more beloved old Zelda games - or Nintendo games - to replicate this nostalgia-driven effect. Are there other Zelda games that have the pull of Ocarina of Time that haven't been remade or remastered already in some capacity?

#3859. The hills are alive with The Sound of Fury, a fantasy musical hack 'n' slash about weaponising pianos to fight the Devil

My firstest-ever Golden Joystick Awards, which took place last night in London, was marred somewhat by 1) a gin & tonic costing eleven quid and 2) my view of the stage being directly obscured by its own rigging. Nonetheless, I did crane enough to get a good view at the reveal of The Sound of Fury, a musically-minded hack 'n' slash in which a troubled classical musician descends into Hell to save a friend from the Devil.

It's not out until late 2027, and the strength of its monster-battering will of course lay in how it feels in the hand. I like the look of this one, though. While it doesn't appear to be a full-on rhythm action game in the Hi-Fi Rush or Dead as Disco vein, it's clearly trying incorporate our glum hero's virtuosity with both visual and thematic flair: spinning attacks are accentuated by trails of sheet music staves, and at least one move inflicts enemies with uncontrollable bouts of dancing. Weapons also take the form of instruments, the trailer being particularly keen to show grand pianos being powerbombed into demon heads. "You dropped your... keys," I will say, to the demons. Heh heh heh.

Also of note is The Sound of Fury's unusual interpretation of Hell, which rather than the usual Biblical/Nordic/Ancient Greek depictions we get in games, is a washed-out mashup of what the Steam page calls "humanity's darkest chapters." Thus, you fight not red-skinned horned imps but gasmasked soldiers and Klu Klux Klansmen, with history-spanning anomalies distorting an otherwise 19th century-flavoured fantasyscape. The laws of time evidently aren't followed here, not least when the protag whips out a Flying V guitar to give the Grim Reaper a different kind of axe wound.

I can't find much else out about developers and self-publishers Games By Wojtek, with that pluralisation assuming 'they' aren't just one person named Wojtek, but The Sound of Fury looks to be his/their debut game. Hopefully it gets a demo, in due course, so we can try tickling its ivories ourselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The BBC reports that Arion Kurtaj, who hacked Rockstar and dumped a massive trove of content from Grand Theft Auto 6 more than a year before it was formally revealed, has pleaded guilty to that and other hacks carried out while he was a member of the Lapsus$ hacking group.

Kurtaj's hack of Rockstar was notable not for the GTA 6 infodump that followed, but because of how it was carried out: With an Amazon Fire Stick, a mobile phone, and a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, connected to a TV in a Travelodge hotel room where he was being held under police protection because of threats against him made by rival hackers over stolen bitcoin.

A 2023 assessment found Kurtaj had "acute autism" and was determined to return to "cybercrime" as soon as possible, despite the fact that he was literally standing trial for doing cybercrimes. Because of that, the jury was asked to determine if he had committed the hacks (it found he had) but not whether he had done so with criminal intent; he was subsequently sentenced to an indefinite stay at a secure hospital, where he would remain unless and until doctors determined that he was no longer a danger.

As we noted at the time, "danger" might seem a bit of a strong word for someone who leaked videogame footage, but the Lapsus$ group had also hacked Microsoft, Samsung, Nvidia and UK telecom company BT&EE, and stole millions in cryptocurrency from individuals. Kurtaj was also reportedly violent while in hospital custody, causing "dozens" of reports of injuries or property damage. In July 2026, that 'no longer a danger' determination was presumably made, as Kurtaj was released from hospital and moved to prison to await retrial.

He has now pleaded guilty to multiple hacks carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old, including the Rockstar hack that led to the GTA 6 leak. He also pleaded guilty to assaults on workers while in custody, which the BBC report says included "multiple biting incidents."

As I said when Kurtaj was moved from hospital to prison, the whole thing strikes me as odd. The big question is how Kurtaj's state of mind at the time of the crimes will influence the outcome of his guilty plea, given that a previous court determined that he needed multiple years of institutionalization. BBC tech reporter Joe Tidy, who's been following the case since Kurtaj's transfer, also described it as "an unusual move" in his report.

Coincidentially, one must assume, Grand Theft Auto 6 launches for consoles on November 19. Kurtaj will be sentenced at a future date. The leaker who goes by Cyberleek, who recently distributed several GTA 6 gameplay videos apparently taken with a development build of the game, remains at large.

#3857. Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Ascendance expansion may be getting a beta, some curious Steam backend updates suggest

Monster Hunter Wilds's first expansion, Ascendance, is set for release sometime next year. But, judging by some very suspect recent changes to the Wilds beta app on Steam, we may be playing some of the new stuff earlier than we thought.

On Steam, Capcom quietly updated the Monster Hunter Wilds Beta app to now say Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test. You can see the change log on SteamDB (via PC Gamer), which also shows an updated key art - all signs that point towards an impending beta for Ascendance.

The beta app is the same one those who played the original Wilds beta had in their library. Though the app was removed following the beta's conclusion, because the two share the same ID, the beta should be visible in users' list of played games under the new name. This could mean players won't need to sign up for the supposed Ascendance beta, seemingly only needing to download the new client.

Seeing as Ascendance itself doesn't have a release date, beyond a nebulous 2027 target, it's hard to speculate when Capcom plans to release the beta. Sometime early in 2027 would be a good guess, perhaps alongside a release date announcement.

Capcom has shown off Ascendance on multiple occasions, more recently in Sony's September State of Play, where we got to see a number of the expansion's new features. A few days later at Tokyo Game Show, we got a first look at returning Elder Dragon Teostra, which we can hunt in the expansion.

Capcom is keen for Ascendance to deliver the level of challenge Monster Hunter is known for, following feedback that the launch version of Wilds simply lacked that expected level of difficulty. While post-launch updates have certainly raised the level of challenge, Ascendance looks to be the next step up.

#3856. Cartoon-styled "lite-vania" Lola's Familiars: Prison of Argnoh will have you springing yourself, and your summoned pals, from magic jail

Andy Dufresne never thought to use witchcraft, did he

Since we're already sharing trailers from non-Geoff awards shows, here's another: a first in-motion look at Lola's Familiars: Prison of Argnoh, a 2D side-scroller and "lite-vania" that sees its shy witch-in-training making her first summonable friends. Then, borrowing their powers to bust out of a dark fantasy oubliette.

It looks like this'll be a mix of passively familiar-enhanced punching and more active, mayhaps traditionally Metroid-y power upgrades, Lola's ghastly pals looming over her tiny frame when called upon. It's all presented in a hand-drawn, lightly anime-ish style, complete with a story setup straight out of Saturday morning TV – Lola's only stuck in Skullcatraz because of a summoning-gone-wrong that occurred in pursuit of her school's unlikely Ofsted-compliant 'familiar contest'. I've attended school several times, and will attest that non-sporting contests, which students remain unaware of until seeing a poster for them, do not exist outside of childrens' television*.

This doesn't seem to be kid fodder, though. Lola's a bean but the familiars, and the prison's other denizens, are growling towers of jaws and decaying flesh. Developers Caracal Games are promising they'll star in a "heartfelt and emotionally resonant story about growth," to balance out the grimness, though I'm less clear on a following blurb point that declares it a "lite-vania," into which you'll "dive into exploration, trial-and-error and platforming, without feeling frustrated." While this might just be an attempt to assuage fears that this'll a Hollow Knight- or Nine Sols-style controller-thrower, I do wonder how one goes light on 'vania. Maybe some of the ability gates open if you just ask them nicely?

That aside, I'm already quite charmed by Lola's Familiars, especially the designs of its bag-eyed wallflower of a heroine and her contrastingly hench minions. Release date is TBC, but the Steam page is up.

*Granted, no TV example was ever as egregiously misleading as Jack Black vehicle School of Rock, which convinced me - then a barely-pubescent aspiring bassist - that winning a local Battle of the Bands would pay out thousands in cash, as opposed to the drinks rounds and packs of guitar strings I'd end up competing for a few years later.

#3855. Clair Obscur Studio Has Lost One of Its Most Important Developers

Jennifer Svedberg-Yen was the narrative lead on Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. She basically shaped the game's twisting and turning story, which many would argue is its greatest asset.

And so it's a bit of a gut punch to hear that she actually left developer Sandfall Interactive earlier this year — meaning that, unless she's already helped establish some of the project's narrative groundwork, she won't be involved with the studio's next game.

Svedberg-Yen dropped this bombshell in an interview with Gamesbeat, having just won a 'Breakthrough US' award at the BAFTAs for her work on Clair Obscur.

"I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition. We’ve parted ways," she explains.

It should be stressed that Svedberg-Yen really did spearhead the Game of the Year-winning title's story and tone right from the start; it wouldn't have been the experience that it was without her.

"I was the third person on the team. The team didn’t exist, actually. When I joined it was two guys who were still working at Ubisoft," she explains.

"The studio didn’t exist. It was the two co-founders and then me. Then we brought in the composer, and then the art director. Several months later we brought in the third co-founder, and then several months after that started the studio. So I was one of the founding members of the team."

Svedberg-Yen continues: "We came up with the idea together from the very start. It was always, from the very beginning, a narrative-focused game. It’s a narrative-first game. That’s what the creative director always said as well. Narrative is king."

And that approach is clear to see in the finished product, which has been lauded for its plot and characters ever since its release back in April of last year.

Svedberg-Yen goes on to talk about how important it is to establish narrative cohesion right off the bat, so that the whole development cycle is built around one vision. She thinks that too many games see story as something that can be slotted in over time, or simply added later on — and the whole thing suffers for it.

As for her own creative process, Svedberg-Yen provides some interesting insight: "I don’t think I could have written something like Expedition in my 20s, or even my 30s."

"I very much believe that one of the most powerful things we can do to train our ability to tell a good story is actually to live a rich life, to observe others, to learn how people work. If you’re trying to write about people, you must understand people."

Svedberg-Yen intends to work on her own projects going forward, which includes writing for film and TV — but she's also passionate about promoting the importance of narrative in video games.

As such, she wants to set up some kind of initiative, helping narrative-focused creatives make the next step in getting their games funded, and in turn, reshape the wider industry's perspective when it comes to storytelling. Sounds like a pretty noble goal to me.

Still, with everything Clair Obscur achieved in terms of narrative, you'd think that Svedberg-Yen will be difficult to replace.

We know that Sandfall Interactive is in the very early stages of developing its next title, but beyond vague, teasing statements, nothing has been made official just yet.

What do you make of this departure? What did you think of Clair Obscur's narrative? Ponder what comes next in the comments section below.
