#3854. GTA 6 review: "An open world with truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality awaits"

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments.

Whoever approved putting the high-end vehicle fence next to a busy interstate should be in jail

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

It was around the 80-hour mark that the panic started to set in. I thought I had done and seen it all. Ran narcotics across the Leonida Keys. Exiled myself from Port Gellhorn. Fought bikers in Ambrosia. Joined a cult. Robbed banks. Partied. I created a life worth living in the heart of Vice City.

Jason and Lucia's story may have been over, but an adventure of my own was just beginning. While I had accomplished a lot in GTA 6, I never did find the time to refuel my beloved '65 Vapid Dominator and drive the long, winding roads up to Lummox County. It's astonishing to think so much time could be spent exploring Leonida, only for its northern border to remain something of a mystery.

Then again, there are still so many mysteries left for me to solve.

So many incidental interactions that have the capacity to spiral into pure carnage. Diversions to discover that may lead to utter disarray. There are streets I've yet to set foot on, and shops I still haven't visited in my hours-long search for a quality leather jacket. There's at least one financial institution that I haven't yet figured out how to escape from without five-stars' worth of VCPD officers shooting me to smithereens.

I fear I may never see or experience all that this world has to offer. And yet, after 13 years of waiting for a new Grand Theft Auto game, perhaps that's the way it should be.

Going from a fan at GTA 4's midnight launch to professionally covering the series has been a career highlight, including reviewing GTA 5 in X360 magazine. I'm never more than a few moments from diving back into Rockstar's worlds. After finishing GTA 6's story, I'm now well past 100 hours still exploring Leonida, using a PS5 Pro code provided by the publisher. – Reviewer Josh West

There are precious few development studios who are willing to play in these sorts of contemporary urban environments. Such is the inherent complexity of regulating an underlying simulation where even the simplest act creates such a wide array of possible consequences. Rockstar Games hasn't just set a new benchmark; it has delivered what is undoubtedly the highest-fidelity sandbox in existence.

How Rockstar has been able to build something of this scale, scope, and quality will be dissected for years to come. It's easy to marvel at the near total lack of loading screens, the speed of character switching, and an exceedingly stable performance with minimal pop-in – despite absurd population density and the speeds at which you may traverse such a topographically diverse playspace.

These aspects are certainly impressive, but they aren't what ultimately elevates GTA 6 into being such a singular experience. Rather, there's a maturity behind the ethos of its core mechanical design, a cohesion in the way that its systems combine, which helps separate it from what the studio has accomplished in the past. In GTA 6, you can feel Rockstar's relentless pursuit of iteration, and the studio's ambition to create the most grounded instalment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise to date.

GTA 6 has the potential to be exceedingly divisive, particularly for those whose only point of interaction with the series thus far has been GTA 5. The life of crime you build for yourself in Leonida is far less chaotic and caustic than the adventures splattered throughout the streets of San Andreas. If the 2013 instalment was a faint echo of a Michael Bay blockbuster, then its successor is more Michael Mann – no less entertaining, but more considerate in how action feeds carnage and frames characters.

Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos – partners in crime, ensnared in a criminal conspiracy that quickly outstrips their understanding of an underworld that they once played in for idle thrills. The dual-protagonist foundation works exceedingly well for GTA 6, allowing you the space to grapple with two distinct personalities who are, in a sense, eternally bound to one another. You get to decide why that may be on a daily basis – for family, for honor, or for the simple promise of a bigger payday.

The interplay between the two characters – born through a combination of nuanced writing, strong performances, and intricate character animations – feeds what is perhaps the most realistic and adult portrayal of a romantic relationship in video game history. Everyday acts of kindness bring Jason and Lucia together, indifference drives them apart. This isn't captured as part of some tawdry in-game checklist, but through deliberate, empathetic actions.

Everyday acts of kindness bring Jason and Lucia together, and indifference drives them apart

In GTA 5, all that L2 was ever good for was aiming a weapon – in GTA 6, it also lets you hold hands with your partner. Interactions only get more detailed from there. Check in with each other over the phone, hit the gym together, hustle drunks at bars, or raid banks with his-and-hers matching tactical rifles. The connection you organically foster between the two characters (or allow to decay) only fuels a more considerate narrative that acts as a catalyst for endless free-flowing excursions across Leonida.

The thematic coherence necessitated by the narrative arc acts as a foundation, feeding other critical changes to the way Grand Theft Auto has traditionally played. If Jason and Lucia's relationship feels real, then so too should the world they express themselves within.

You can only carry two handguns and two longarms at a time, for example, and brandishing a weapon will cause the public to react in different, volatile ways. Police presence isn't some glorified cone of vision, but rather it works as a communicative force to be feared – able to track your appearance, vehicles, and criminal activities between city limits. All of this (and more) contributes to a feeling of true, immersive role-play within Leonida.

With Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar Games sought to create a reactive virtual world. The studio aspired to near-total immersion – action, interactions, and character development feeding off the sandbox's simulation of an everyday reality. In that sense, GTA 6 is a true sequel to RDR2. Rockstar has pursued relentless iteration of those Old West foundations here, leaning into those immersive qualities where it makes sense for the criminal-fantasy GTA fosters, and pulling back when they don't.

Unlike RDR2's Arthur Morgan, your hair and beard won't naturally grow over time. Weight and health fluctuations are less severe. Eating and exercising will impact the definition of Jason and Lucia's bodies, and resting helps to ease the exhaustive toll of constant criminality, but you'll never find yourself entirely at the mercy of these systems. Engagement with the Vice City lifestyle simply helps further the feeling that you are living life on your own terms.

Rockstar has gone to great lengths to inject more "freedom and flexibility" into its main mission design, all in an effort to reduce the number of fail states you encounter for daring to be experimental.

GTA 6 also features a more nuanced version of the Red Dead Redemption 2 honor system, with your reputation fed throughout the world more organically. It's one of the more fascinating new systems, and a sharp diversion from prior games in the series that have never really commented on your criminality. Criminal Profiles are built gradually over time, ranging from Professional to Irredeemable, based on the way you commit crimes and handle pressure.

The improvements to graphical fidelity and animation quality, and the lengths Rockstar has gone to create a virtual world with a functioning ecology, have meant that there are more human reactions from the populace to your presence than ever before. This intersects well with the Criminal Profile system, which (while never overly judgemental) does gradually convince you to define a moral compass and follow your own value system.

There was a point where I realized that I had inadvertently sunk the entirety of my BuckMe bank account into an arsenal dedicated entirely to stealth action. I was raiding banks, drug labs, and gang compounds like GTA 6 was some sort of perverse Florida-set Metal Gear Solid. Sneaking my way into cover and onto rooftops, tracing enemy patrol patterns with a cigarette in one hand and silenced pistol in the other. I'd like to tell you that smoking before every firefight was because it temporarily boosts the Focus bar, but at some point I had become addicted to the aesthetic of it all.

A stealth-action approach to encounters in GTA 6 worked in my favor because I was pursuing a Professional criminal profile – assigned by the worldwide reputation system for those who lean towards non-lethal incapacitations and clean getaways. I gravitated towards this style of play because of the Focus system, which iterates smartly on aspects of RDR's Eagle Eye and Max Payne's Bullet Time. Skillfully shooting weapons out of hands, or capping enemies in the knee before watching them tumble down staircases in slow motion, is just as satisfying as striding out of cover with a shotgun.

Combat is one of many aspects where Rockstar has built precipitously beyond GTA 5. Placing bullets requires real aiming and precision. Weapon feedback is weighty, with each weapon type and manufacturer variant carrying its own unique handling profile. Survival requires movement and cover. Improvements have been made to the driving models too, with narrower streets necessitating more dexterity behind the wheel – not to mention countless more variables at play, from the threat of running out of fuel to the scores of modifications that can be applied to your favorite cars.

There are degrees of sophistication to everything that GTA 6 does. There isn't an aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments. It's a little slower and certainly more balanced, but no less entertaining. It's immediately noticeable that the artificial intelligence guiding the actions of both your partner and the NPCs who inhabit Vice City is greatly improved too, with some of GTA 6's best moments coming as you ask Jason to take the wheel while you lean out of a window as Lucia, a chattering assault rifle chewing through the tyres and rotary blades of a pursuing police force.

If more nuanced storytelling has the potential to be divisive, then the revisions to the Wanted and Heat systems could be downright controversial. The police are more attuned to your actions than ever, actively tracking a number of variables at any one time in an effort to curtail crimes both big and small.

The return of a six-star wanted level is great for those looking for more of a challenge, although the Heat system – which can identify you after a crime based on factors such as your appearance, vehicle, outfit, visible weapon, partner's appearance, and whether you were recorded by CCTV – introduces a whole new dynamic to Grand Theft Auto. Some will love it, others will hate it.

This system can fluctuate between being a little frustrating (particularly at lower Wanted levels, for more incidental infractions) and utterly thrilling once the pressure is on, particularly if you're holding hundreds of thousands of dollars in stolen jewellery, marked bills, and narcotics between Jason, Lucia, and the storage of their personal vehicle – loot is lost if not properly funnelled through fences. And when the Heat and Wanted system are on your back, it evokes this almost desperate pressure to survive a city that is collapsing in on you.

There's a sort of useful friction introduced through the revised Wanted and Heat system, overlapping with more freeform opportunities presented throughout the world itself. While GTA 5 is best remembered for its cinematic, structured heists, its successor finds its best moments as you decide on a whim to stick up a gas station or start smashing up the display cabinets in a jewelry store whilst you're between objectives. Bank robberies present massive opportunity and carry enormous risk, necessitating careful, tactile preparation before you burst through doors with weapons raised.

The high-speed pursuits which can unfurl out of these encounters get gradually more out of control until they don't – Busted, Wanted, or free to fight and love for another day. Your Heat level and the world's awareness of your crimes is tracked intuitively on a more dynamic HUD, and I appreciate just how many opportunities there are to escape the police depending on any number of external factors.

One of my favorite escapes saw me fleeing a large bank in Downtown Vice City – a densely populated area with streets packed full of police, pedestrians, and other vehicles. Throwing stash bags to my partner, spilling out of the vault and onto the streets, I was able to gain just a little distance from the cops and pull into a multistory carpark. Precious seconds to hide Jason's weapons in the trunk of his car, swap out Lucia's outfit, and hotwire a new vehicle. Clambering into the car, I manually shut off the headlights and engine, and ducked beneath the steering wheel – the patrolling police passed none the wiser, affording me the space to slip out of the garage slowly.

The sheer scale of Leonida is something to behold. It's a playspace which rewards curiosity and creativity. It's impressive, especially when you remember it has all been "curated, considered, and created by a human hand."

It's these sorts of unscripted sequences where GTA 6 shines brightest, although that isn't to say that the main story isn't packed with its fair share of memorable moments. There will be some debate as to whether the standout GTA 6 heists rise to the levels of GTA 5's 'The Paleto Score' and GTA 4's 'Three Leaf Clover', but they certainly come close.

Core mission design is still cinematic and largely linear by design, although you do have wider space to experiment in approach and escape than in previous Grand Theft Auto games – mission parameters can be broad, and it's up to you to decide how to achieve them. Rockstar has introduced the ability to manually retry a mission from its last checkpoint, further exorcising some of the series' more frustrating demons.

GTA 6 also happens to be exceedingly well-written. Missions may be grounded in the virtual reality of Leonida, but they still have scope to be ridiculous. Mysteries unfurl from QR codes embedded in the world. Snippets from a radio news broadcast can make you laugh in one moment and pay off as a chance encounter in the world some 40 hours later. Random citizens will make you laugh, moments between Jason and Lucia will make you cry. It's a true joy to spend time in this world.

I have Jason and Lucia start their road trip up to Lummox County in Key Lento, just a short drive to the federal penitentiary where they had once served time. Now, it's just the open road. Their favorite outfits packed into the trunk of an over-torqued Vapid Dominator, along with a small arsenal of weapons, ammo crates, body armor, and parachutes.

The sun shines brightly; the radio tuned to V-Rock as hits from the '80s soundtrack a transition from lush ocean views to the quiet character of Hamlet. A quick stop at Sara's Unisex Salon for a fresh cut for Jason, and makeover for Lucia. Later, an unintended diversion into Southside after a small collision on Interstate 97 led an aggravated driver to jackknife my whip and feed bullets into the windshield – a local Pay 'n' Spray draining what little Pocket Cash I had on me for repairs. The sun started to set.

I stop to refuel somewhere around Vice City's Little Cuba district. An eruption of rain washing Lucia's makeup down her face, her gaze fixed entirely on another bay at the garage – a drunk driver pours gasoline into the flatbed of his truck. On the road and out of the city, the subtle changes in landscape reveal a world of contrast and contradictions. The changing colors of police vehicles, the different accents and demeanours of everyday citizens at roadside restaurants, indicate a crossing of boundaries.

Day transitions to night, night back to day. The weather shifting constantly. The vehicle splutters as roads become more uneven the further we cruise away from the big city. I switch from driver to passenger, smoking cigarettes as Jason and Lucia chatter about their lives. Eventually, vast farmlands settle into dense forest canopies beneath the shadow of Mt. Kalaga National Park. It took me 80 hours to see the dense foliage and lush, leafy green hues of Lummox County. And there's no telling how many more hours await me there.

In Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games has created the ultimate time vampire. This is an open-world that is driven entirely by freedom and consequence, where every one of your actions ultimately impacts the lives of Jason and Lucia. GTA 6 invites you to live a life in Leonida. A world that is as beautiful as it is deadly; as full of heart as it is heartbreak. GTA 6 is an essential play for PS5 and Xbox Series X owners.

My GTA 6 review was written based on a PS5 Pro playthrough, with the game code provided to me by Rockstar Games. And it must be said, the improved ray tracing to help bolster lighting and shadow on PS5 Pro is pretty damned delightful. Vice City looks gorgeous at night.

So long as we're clear that I reviewed GTA 6 on PS5 Pro. I was very impressed with the performance. Rockstar targeted 30fps on all platforms, but I didn't encounter any fluctuations. There was infrequent pop-in, but that was only during play sessions which stretched beyond eight hours.

I spent over 100 hours playing GTA 6 for review. The Jason and Lucia story is all wrapped up, all optional missions are done, and I've made some pretty good headway on getting through a lot of the activities. Time to hunt for some collectibles!

I have completed every Grand Theft Auto game. Yes, even the ones released for PS1. I have very fond memories of attending the midnight launch for GTA 4, and even fonder memories of reviewing GTA 5 way back in 2013 for X360 Magazine.

This will be a contentious debate, but there's a very good argument to be made that Grand Theft Auto 6 is the best Rockstar game. It's certainly a better overall experience than GTA 5, and more entertaining than Red Dead Redemption 2.

#3853. Conan: The Black Pyramid shoves the titular barbarian into a very Hades-inspired action roguelite with the addition of a few other familiar heroes

I feel like one thing I only sort of miss from my youth, viewed through the lenses of those rose tinted goggles, is the established intellectual property game that just copies the formula of another, successful game. Obviously there are plenty of genres that are trendy to imitate, but how often do you see something that's just sort of "thing you know slapped on top of game you know?" Perhaps that's a tad mean, but I do genuinely have a fondness for such games, so I'm quite pleased by the announcement of Conan: The Black Pyramid, an action roguelite RPG that so clearly went to Supergiant Games' School of Hades you have to admire the boldness just a little bit.

Conan: The Black Pyramid puts you in the hotseat as the titular barbarian, of course, but also as other characters from the series like Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and apparently, more! So, immediately, a notable enough difference from Hades, and one that seems like a neat take. As one of them you then "Descend into eldritch chambers of the Black Pyramid, a mysterious and dangerous place that defies the logic of space and time. Confront the shadows of the champions themselves and piece together the dark secrets of their past."

Where it is similar to Hades lies in the fact that the titular triangle changes in form each time you go in it, and of course there are different abilities and buffs to pick up along the way to aid you in your quest. Each character has their own combination of weapons and abilities, so it does sound like you can mix it up quite nicely. There is, also, 2-player online co-op (sorry to the couch lovers, I suppose), adding to the ways it differs and making it a tad more friendly for those that have exactly one friend who also loves Conan.

Overall, seems like a fresh enough take on Hades while still trying to find some amount of its own identity. And hey, Hades is great, so I'm never upset about having a little bit more of that kind of game. No release date attached to Conan: The Black Pyramid just yet, but it is planned to arrive sometime in 2027. You can check it out on Steam here.

#3852. World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunters have found the MMO's first hidden treasure

World of Warcraft secret hunters are a noble breed, known for scouring the MMO for years for hidden trinkets and treasures. With World of Warcraft: Forever's launch, they've uncovered a quest chain for an especially fancy sword.

Over the past week, members of the WoW Secret Hunters Discord found a quest chain that takes place entirely on the Zephras Isle, meaning you'll need to have access to the Skyborne elves to grab this sword. Navigating the island, you'll need to first pick up an ancient heirloom ring from the starting zone. Simple enough!

Then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind. It turns out this torch has uses far beyond this one zone however, as taking it back to the Ruins of Ban'aethal on the Zephras Isle will reward you with a secret quest and the Ancient Hilt.

With the hilt and ring, you then must track down an Ancient Blade from one of several spawn locations on the Zephras Isle. Once you finally track it down, that's the end of part one of this quest chain. You get the sword: Eluvi'ana, which on its own isn't particularly strong, but is speculated to be upgraded later down the line.

You then need to get a corrupted water globe from either Darkshore or the Blackfathom Deeps dungeon depending on your faction, do a fetch quest for a hidden spirit in Ashenvale, then take your hoard of special quest items to a NPC in the new Shen'Dralar zone.

He won't give you the finished sword. Instead he sends you to gather more items from higher-level zones. You'll need to raid a secluded vault in Feralas that you can only see with the Ancient Hilt, dive underwater in Azshara, and kill Highborne Shades in Winterspring. Once you've done all that, you can then cleanse the orb up in Hyjal, speak to the fella back in Shen'Dralar, then shimmy over to the end game Dire Maul dungeon to speak to Prince Tortheldrin about *another* sword.

This is how far the World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunter community has gotten to. It's believed that grinding up the Shen'dralar reputation to Honoured is required for the next step, as Prince Tortheldrin pretty much says as much in his dialogue. So the hunt is still on!

These sorts of secrets make up an important part of any good MMO: the solving of mysteries in these vast digital open worlds. In retail WoW, I have fond memories of the Waist of Time quest chain, which was an arduous and comical grind for a fancy belt during the Battle for Azeroth expansion. This secret sword quest chain may very well evolve into something as legendary as that, at least I hope so!

If you're not already playing it, World of Warcraft: Forever is plenty of fun. A record-breaking number of players are making the journey through Azeroth right now, diving into quests and dungeons new and old.

The only answer we have right now is that Rockstar has not announced GTA 6 Online. But we all know it's totally going to have a multiplayer mode, right? #3850. Spyro's New PS5 Game Teases Appearance at This Year's Game Awards

Publisher Activision and developer Toys for Bob are teasing Spyro: A Realm Beyond will be part of The Game Awards 2026.

In just a few weeks, the upcoming platformer starring everyone's favourite purple dragon will get a public showing for the first time since its announcement back in June.

As reported by Gematsu, an email from Activision makes it pretty clear we'll be seeing more of the game during the event.

"[The Game Awards 2026] are around the corner, and Spyro is getting fired up," it says. "Before we get there, here's a look at some of the Spyro: A Realm Beyond assets [of the Painted Plains area] you might have sneaked a peek at in [Xbox’s 25th anniversary] commemorative magazine. Who is ready to see more of the first all-new Spyro adventure in nearly 20 years? Sheep beware."

The assets the message mentions are new screenshots alongside concept art of the same areas. Here they are:

As well as this email, official Spyro social accounts have begun hinting at Game Awards activity:

It's not known exactly what we're going to see, but hopefully we'll get our first proper look at the game in action.

Spyro: A Realm Beyond is the first all-new game in close to 20 years, and while the Reignited Trilogy remake is great, it'll be awesome to see the series make a real return.

Are you excited to see more of this one? Tell us in the comments section below.

#3848. As of this week, PlayStation 5 has surpassed 100 million consoles sold

PlayStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed. The milestone was reached on 10th November, almost exactly six years on from the console's launch.

The figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers. In other words, the number of PS5s in people's homes is smaller than that 100m.

Nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022. It also means the PS5 has almost matched the original PlayStation in units sold (102.4m). As impressive as the numbers are, historical data shows that PS5 sales have been in decline.

Sony hasn't shied away from discussing that fact in its earnings reports. 2.6m PS5 consoles were sold during the most recent quarter (Q2 of FY2026), well below the 4m sold over the same period the year prior. In fact, Q2 of FY2026 is the lowest second quarter on record in terms of units sold since the PS5's launch.

However, it's also worth noting that, small though it may be, the second quarter's result is higher than the first quarter's 1.6m, the second-lowest of any single quarter since the PS5's launch, beaten only by Q4 of FY2025's 1.5m.

If numbers don't recover in the third and fourth quarters, this may be the PS5's lowest year ever in terms of units sold. Although the second quarter's sales boost can be attributed to the high anticipation of Grand Theft Auto 6, the overall downturn is largely due to the console's higher price; Sony raised the PS5 and PS5 Pro's prices on several occasions since 2020. The company's bottom line, however, hasn't been affected much, as its plan to generate more revenue from its already-engaged audience continues to work.

"Rockstar Games was founded on the belief that games could achieve the same distinction as all other forms of storytelling"

GTA 6 is finally here. The long-awaited sequel arrives 13 years after the release of GTA 5 for PS3 and Xbox 360. It's a moment worth celebrating. Clearly, Rockstar Games feels the same way, as the studio's elusive co-founder and president makes a rare statement to help welcome you to Leonida.

"Rockstar Games was founded on the belief that games could achieve the same distinction as all other forms of storytelling, become essential to modern culture, and to be thought of as stories and worlds that live on with us," says Houser, in a comment released to GamesRadar+.

"This week, Grand Theft Auto returns to Leonida and modern-day Vice City. While things have changed and time has passed, one aspect holds true: We have tried to create an experience that will exceed your expectations while showing what this medium is capable of, and why we believe games are so special."

Houser has an executive producer credit on every mainline installment of the Grand Theft Auto series, and has served as a central creative lead and source of truth within the studio. He knows better than most just how important Rockstar's sprawling virtual worlds are to players, and the breadth of interest this return to Vice City will attract around the world. It's a challenge he doesn't take lightly.

"Whether you can trace your journey to this game through the entire series or are experiencing Grand Theft Auto for the first time, this is a narrative set in a world of possibilities – and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels, and concludes. We hope it feels both familiar and entirely new, and above all, we hope you have fun." Houser's statement concludes: "We look forward to many more years of sharing these experiences with you."

Many more years is right. While Grand Theft Auto 6 has launched as a single-player-only experience (and the studio is yet to officially comment on whether a successor to GTA Online is in development), I can say from my own personal experience with the game that it presents the sort of reactive world which will have the capacity to surprise and delight for years to come.

You can read my full, spoiler-free GTA 6 review to learn more about Rockstar Games' exceedingly impressive creation ahead of its November 19, 2026 release on PS5 and Xbox Series X.

#3846. Barbie Rewind, out now, invites you to take a trip down memory lane with a whole bunch of life in plastic classics, and one game that was previously unreleased

Is there a character not originally from a video game that has more games than Barbie? Maybe! I don't want to do any maths right now, but there aren't many that could touch her on sheer numbers. She's had all sorts of digital adventures, her games having a huge influence on the world of 'girl games'. As complicatedly gendered that may now be, the significance can't be understated, and as of today you can have a romp through a nice portion of that history in Barbie Rewind, a compilation of almost two decades worth of games all wrapped up in a nice little decorating game.

The latest release from Digital Eclipse, aficionados of digital multi-pack games like Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration and last year's Mortal Kombat: Legacy Kollection, Barbie Rewind has a total of 16 games from across the doll's video game history. Starting all the way back in 1991 with Barbie for the original NES, it jumps around to the Game Boy Color with Barbie: Pet Rescue, to the SNES with Barbie: Vacation Adventure. That last one's important because it's actually an unreleased game, making it quite a neat addition to the package.

Beyond that, there's the customizable DreamHouse, where you get a whole bunch of furniture to deck it out with. Nothing overly complicated here, it's just a thematically appropriate appendage that helps to recreate the feeling of playing with a doll house in pixel art form. Expect familiar faces like Ken, Teresa and Christie to pop up here and there as well. You'll also find a digital lookbook where you can "flip through the pages of Barbie history."

Perhaps slightly disappointingly you won't find a number of beloved Barbie games like Barbie: Secret Agent or Barbie Horse Adventures: Mystery Ride. A lot of the games in this package are the 2D, pixel art entries, so that was probably meant to be the focus here. Hopefully someone will part those 3D releases somewhere down the line! In any case, if you fancy a trip down memory lane, you can pick up Barbie Rewind on Steam now.

The US president doesn't seem too concerned about the potential risks to US national security: "I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A CNBC report says the return of disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang is not being considered by Nvidia's board of directors, despite a rising chorus of billionaire voices calling for it—including, earlier today, that of US president Donald Trump.

"I would not mind. I would not mind that," Trump told reporters in response to a question about Huang's possible return (via Reuters). "I like—I threw out the name of Tim Cook. But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement—I think he learned a big lesson, I guess. Maybe one lesson's more important than another. But I would certainly not mind seeing that."

Asked about US intelligence reports that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Trump said he doesn't know whether she's a spy, and that "a lot of people" are asking Huang to return to the CEO's role.

"They think Jensen should go back," Trump said. "That certainly isn't a bad idea." He also said that US national security was not put at risk by Huang's deep ties to Trump, adding that "China plays games with us, so we play games with China."

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, shortly after his affairs with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence as well as multiple Nvidia employees came to light. Calls for his return were almost immediate, mostly notably from billionaires like Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, but also Nvidia employees and fans. Tech executives have reportedly launched a "war room" to lobby for his return, and Huang himself is apparently open to the idea.

Whether Nvidia feels the same is another matter: An anonymous source told CNBC that the board is not considering bringing him back, and is instead focusing on an investigation into Huang's affairs and whether he compromised US national security or Nvidia itself.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, one of Trump's most vocal and reliable supporters, also recently seemed to dismiss the idea, saying Nvidia "needed a dramatic shakeup" at the top and that it should look "outside the company" for a new chief executive. It remains to be seen whether any of those positions change in light of Trump's support.

#3844. Cover your robot body in magical fungus aplenty and galavant across a mystical, Soulslike world in MycoRelic, now out in 1.0

Robot, robot, robot, robot, mushroom! Mushroom!

I often find it quite dull that the main takeaway far too many people have taken from Dark Souls, aside from thinking that the most interesting thing is its combat, is that it's all so bloomin' grimdark. I'm not saying I need sunshine and rainbows, I'd just like a vibe that's even remotely trying to be different from FromSoftware's seminal work. And so! I am quite pleased to discover MycoRelic, a Soulslike that pits you as a robot that covers its body in mushroom parts that offer elemental powers.

MycoRelic, from the offset, has this low-poly style that almost reminds me of oldschool RuneScape in a way I clown with quite quickly. The game looks good! The vibes look odd and, thankfully, not particularly derivative of medieval aesthetics. But while I am vibes-first when it comes to games, a Soulslike does live and die by its systems, and the systems here sound quite intriguing.

For starters, there are no classes to speak of, just various weapons with their own moves and stats, and armour that "suits your playstyle and aesthetic." Huzzah! A game that understands one of the best bits of Dark Souls is dressing up. When you start out, you just have a "decrepit, moldy frame," but over time you can replace parts of it to improve your health, stamina, frame integrity, and the "potency of your fungal magic." Mycellic music to my ears.

Different fungi have different powers, and can be combined to create new effects, or used in a multitude of ways; healing water can restore your friends or put out a fire for example. And oh, yes, there's co-op too, though I don't know if it's the friction-heavy Dark Souls kind or the seamless, hassle-free kind. On top of all this you've got an air-dash and can glide too, offering up some tasty platforming potential not typically found in the genre. I like it! And it just came out in 1.0 after a period of early access. If you fancy giving it a go, there's still a demo on Steam, or you can just pick up the full thing.

#3843. "I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released" - former Tekken director Katsuhiro Harada trashes Microsoft's console in front of senior Xbox staff

Katsuhiro Harada, formerly director on the Tekken series, is known for not pulling his punches. This truth was reinforced recently, as he said he wished the Xbox Series S "wouldn't be released" at a developer panel. All while a member of the Xbox team was in the room.

Per Inven Global, Harada was sitting on a panel at the Console Game Developers Conference 2026 in South Korea. The panel was moderated by former Sony president Shuhei Yoshida, and featured Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee (Stellar Blade), Too Kyo Games CEO Kazutaka Kodaka (Dangenrompa), CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko (Cyberpunk 2077), Ludeon Studios CEO Tynan Sylvester (Rimworld), and of course CEO of the newly formed VS Studio Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken).

The panel were asked about the advantages of console development, as well as specific challenges when creating games for certain platforms. Harada led the charge, speaking to the advantages consoles provide for fighting game developers, as the hardware is ideal for tournaments and esports events. Following this, he took an opportunity to speak about a console that drew his ire.

"That said, there's something I really want to say while I have the floor. Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released," Harada said (translations to English via Inven Global). Harada then asked Sasko from the CD Projekt Red team whether he was "upset inside" because of the Xbox Series S.

Sasko proceeded to "burst out laughing" according to Inven Global, before responding: "It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada followed up with additional thoughts: "You just used a very polite and elegant way to say "Xbox Series S sucks," right? (laughs) Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child.

"Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Sasko stepped up to offer some perks to the Series S. While he agreed that many players the full technical context behind the Series S' weaknesses, he pointed out that optimisation for weaker hardware like the Series S made games run "significantly better" across all platforms. He even had a Cyberpunk 2077 example, as optimisation work done for the Switch 2 version were applied to all platforms "to great effect". Sasko also pointed to the affordability side of the argument, saying that the cheaper price of the Series S allows for market expansion.

Harada responded: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Here, Shift Up's DongKi Lee ended the topic with some optimism for Microsoft's future consoles: "Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Earlier this year Harada founded Vs Studio with SNK's support, with other veterans from Bandai Namco's Tekken team hopping on board for whatever it's working on. As for the Xbox Helix consoles, in this current hardware environment with bloated costs for RAM and other components, it's reportedly looking a tad expensive. Maybe a Series S equivalent is on the cards?

#3842. GTA 6 PS5 Trophies Revealed, 100% Completion Needed for the Platinum

GTA 6 is currently going live across the world, and in doing so, its PS5 Trophy list has now been made public. Exophase has the full list, which comprises 55 Trophies, including a Platinum Trophy.

The big thing here is that — just like every other Rockstar title released from PS3 onwards — you'll need to achieve 100% completion to unlock every Trophy.

I've looked through the complete list, and there's nothing there I'd consider a spoiler; the Trophy names and descriptions are vague, so don't worry about having the ending spoiled or anything like that.

As stated, a Gold Trophy called A Long Road wants you to "attain 100% completion". Given how much content is packed into GTA 6, this could take you hundreds of hours to accomplish.

Alongside the requirements of the 100% completion, you've obviously got to complete the main story, win races and complete stunts, finish missions for specific characters (which I assume are side quests), and also succeed in an assortment of robberies.

"The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto 6"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's a truly astonishing level of detail presented all throughout Leonida. For all the pre-release conversation about whether Rockstar Games should have considered lowering the visual fidelity of its largest, most reactive sandbox to date in favor of performance boosts, the immersive qualities of this space are one of the standout aspects of GTA 6.

I can say this with some confidence, having spent well over one hundred hours exploring Vice City in support of my spoiler-free GTA 6 review. In a statement released to GamesRadar+, the vice president of art and environment at Rockstar asserts that "the life is in the detail" of this astonishing open-world.

"The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied. The personalization of each home and business so that it all feels unique and there's no repetition," says Adam Cochrane.

He adds: "Then add into that the vignettes and storytelling the teams have added for the players to explore and discover. Some of these areas have in-game rewards, and some are just rewarding experiences themselves when you see the care and attention that has gone into the creation."

A lot of this detail is almost imperceptible, but it does all ultimately contribute to this feeling that you aren't playing as Jason and Lucia in the world that's been purpose-built to become a home to their criminal activities, but rather that you are living a life of your own design within a world that has some semblance of inherent virtual reality. It's a pretty astonishing thing to spend time in Leonida, as you'll no doubt discover for yourselves on November 19, 2026.

What's especially impressive is that GTA 6 arrives at a time where the video game industry is grappling with the spiralling pressures of creating games in the modern era – where increases in fidelity are placing more demands and expectations onto the shoulders of creative teams than ever before – and with the ethics of utilizing Generative-AI systems to help alleviate these burdens.

Cochrane is quick to remind us that the power of GTA 6 lies in the people who have brought this world to life. "Then you zoom out, and look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realize that the detail you've been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world. Then you realize that it's all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand," he says, before adding, "and you can't quite believe it."

Hark! A new Slay the Spire 2 patch is here! Or, well, it is if you're someone who's trying out the beta branches of the game. If you're not, it might be worth trying out, as Mega Crit say this is their biggest patch for the game so far, with "some really impactful bits of content that will require lots of testing before they reach the main branch."

First up, a new character: The Fool! "Wah!! The first new character for Early Access arrives!" a Steam blog post explains. "A silly musician who wields a bow! The post doesn't go into much detail as to what the new character can actually do, so, you'll have to discover that one for yourself!

There are also two new game modes to try out with this beta update. The first is Blitz, a "condensed and chaotic deckbuilding-focused mode." Here, the "Merchant's wares feel a bit off, the map is gone, and Gold no longer matters." You'll also find it comes with five levels of Ascension shared across every character, and you can unlock it by completing an Ascension run on any difficulty. The second mode is Dread, which as the name implies, is a "brutal" difficulty mode that you can only play if you've reached Ascension 10 on every character, including The Fool. "All ascension modifiers are enabled. Bosses are stronger and buff all enemies in their Act. Curses will also pile up as you climb the Spire. Death is expected."

New events have been added to Underdocks and Act 2 and 3 too. Some nice quality of life alterations have been made, like how the character select screen for standard runs will start on whatever character you played as last, and controller navigation at the Merchant has been improved too. You can read all about the rest of the many changes right here.

#3839. Hell Let Loose's original developers' Napoleonic-era extraction game, Hunger, gets December early access release, and an open beta this month

Good Fun Corp, the studio made up of the original developers behind Hell Let Loose, has finally announced a release date for its anticipated next project: Hunger. The extraction shooter-slasher game enters early access on Steam on 3rd December, and there's good news if you're eager to try it out before then.

Hunger's first and only open beta has also been announced, taking place 27th-29th November, the weekend prior to its early access launch. Unlike past tests, this one is available for anyone who requests access on Steam.

Though it may appear as yet another extraction shooter on the surface, Hunger offers more complex and intertwined systems than most. For one, combat has a focus on melee with only a few intentionally clunky firearms available. Though this is a PvPvE game, the vs environment side includes the sort of puzzle-solving, questing and dungeon-raiding typical of RPGs. The game's alternate history, plague-ravaged European setting gives it a grimey, steel-and-mud look few games have.

Beyond the in-match experience, Good Fun's ambitions extend to Hunger's MMO-style progression, its hub area with distinct characters and varied playable classes - all of which can be sampled in the upcoming beta.

Hunger just came off a very successful closed beta, which clearly didn't suffer by kicking off right alongside Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access. Hunger is currently among Steam's most-wishlisted games, with over 700,000 wishlists, according to the developer.

The launch version includes three large maps, six playable characters, and five Mastery trees with more than 100 Masteries to unlock for your characters. Hunger has only been announced for PC so far, but will presumably arrive on consoles following its early access journey.

The Leviathan, the 111-meter superyacht owned by Valve co-founder Gabe Newell, has a number of unconventional features. It has a pool for SCUBA testing. It has an NBA-regulation basketball court. An Aston-Martin can be found parked on its helipad. It forgoes the typical teakwood deck in favor of easier-to-clean synthetic flooring.

But for the industry experts at Superyacht Times, which recently released a walkthrough video of the Leviathan's features and operating philosophy (via GamesRadar), the most remarkable thing about Newell's roving wave-palace is its owner's willingness to appreciate the crew that enables his lifestyle of seaborne excess.

"The most surprising thing is what happens when we go through these doors," says Superyacht Times editor-in-chief Francesca Webster as she enters into an immaculate communal dining space on the Leviathan's main deck. "Rather than having the traditional saloon which we normally see on a superyacht—welcoming guests and being the first point of contact to the interior—Gabe actually opted to utilize this incredible space for the crew mess."

Instead of banishing his crew to whatever dank closets and canned rat-gruel might be typical for superyacht staff, Newell enjoys his meals alongside the crew each day. According to Superyacht Times, engaging in that sort of mutual humanity makes him a peculiarity among yachtfolk.

"It's all about shared experience on board his boats. And that is something that we've really never seen before in our industry," Webster says.

Having delivered a casual indictment of the pursuit of yachting in its entirety, we move on the Leviathan's owner deck, where we're shown one of a series of VIP cabins that would shame a top-of-the-line hotel. There, we see more of Newell's uncharacteristic acknowledgment that it would maybe be cool for the people who keep a luxury ship running to enjoy some of the luxury.

"One of the most unique things about Gabe, the ownership structure that he has and the way that he has a vision for yachting," Webster says, "is that this VIP cabin is also used by the crew."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

That vision was apparently a head-scratcher for the vessel's designers at Mark Bryman Design, who Webster says "found this to be quite an incredible challenge and an exciting opportunity to think about yachting from a different perspective and really turn the ownership experience on its head."

Given the video's faintly perplexed tone, Superyacht Times still appears somewhat puzzled by the idea. But the Leviathan's designers seem to have gotten a hold on things eventually: In addition to the crew mess and lavish cabins, the yacht also features a gaming center, outfitted with 15 PCs "for the crew, the guests, and Gabe himself to come and enjoy themselves."

The appreciation evidently goes both ways. Superyacht Times says superyachts retain a crewmember for six to nine months, on average. Newell's crews, however, tend to stay on for an average of four and a half years—a figure that would undoubtedly be lower if he never got over his Mongolian throat singing phase.

#3837. Wolfenstein 3 and new id Software game confirmed, as Xbox boss somehow unrelatedly shouts about one person soon wielding "capabilities that once required entire nations"

Asha Sharma had a normal one as Xbox turned 25

Xbox have confirmed that Wolfenstein 3 is indeed in production at Indiana Jones and the Great Circle devs MachineGames and that Doom makers id Software have started work on their next game after losing a bunch of staff to the mass layoffs across Microsoft's gaming division this year.

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations," isn't part of the marketing spiel for either of those games. Instead, it's something Xbox CEO Asha Shama has bellowed amid a rant outlining how she sees the company's future.

The Wolfenstein and id confirmations came as Xbox had a bit of a social media party to commemorate their 25th birthday. Sharma, ever keen to be seen right next to any positive news coming out of the company, confirmed Wolfenstein 3 is in production by posting a photo showing a few lines from its script. Around the same time, she shouted out Doom: The Dark Ages Revelations' incoming Slaughter Mode, adding that "the team is already working on its next game".

The official id Software account responded to note that this next game is being made by their "teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin", and that "it'll be some time before [they're] ready to share more".

We're incredibly excited about our next project, a new game from our teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin. It'll be some time before we're ready to share more but we can't wait for you to see what we're working on.

Alongside hollering about these couple of games, Sharma put out a 25th anniversary statement which for the most part does the sort of bigging up of Xbox's past you'd expect. Good times were had, we blazed a trail and made lots of money, etcetera. The final section saw the exec attempt to look forward to the next 25 years for Xbox.

"While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically," she wrote. "As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this.

"Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

That certainly sounds a lot like the sales pitch the biggest proponents of generative AI keep wheeling out, while avoiding saying generative AI out loud in the hopes of making it more palatable to folks who might not make the connection. I'm waiting for Sharma to put out another post revealing that she accidentally mixed another section of the Wolfenstein script into her celebratory musings, but I'm not holding my breath.

Xbox parent company Microsoft are still currently subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#3836. GTA 6 might be censored in Japan, if the game's smaller install size and lack of "strong sexual content" warning is anything to go by

GTA 6 is finally coming out worldwide next week, putting an end to a 13-year wait and at least one popular meme format, but the highly-anticipated game might look a bit different in Japan.

Now that pre-loading is live for the Rockstar Games mammoth, players across the globe can finally download the game and drool over its icon for the next week or so. But pre-orderers in Japan have noticed that GTA 6's file size comes to about 208GB on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores, versus up to 212GB in other regions.

As reported on by GameSpark and covered by Automaton, the game also received the strictest age rating from the Japanese certification board CERO - "Z" which is recommended for players aged 18 and over - but the listing notably doesn't contain one disclaimer seen in other international ratings.

PEGI and ESRB both warn of the game's "strong sexual content." Curiously, CERO's rating includes no such disclaimer. Together, some fans have taken the lack of "sexual content" disclaimer and smaller file size as signs that GTA 6 might not include some of the risque content we know it'll flaunt elsewhere in the world - based on NSFW leaks and a past rating that already clued us into the fact GTA 6 might be the first GTA to feature full-on sex scenes.

The potential regional censorship isn't too surprising, though, considering how trimmed down GTA 5's Japanese release was at the time. Rockstar had to remove and alter a bunch of GTA 5 scenes to comply with the country's normally strict content guidelines, including Trevor's controversial torture segment and multiple scenes featuring nudity. Baldur's Gate 3, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and many more have been subject to similar restrictions in the past.

Earlier this week, GTA 6 became the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation and Xbox's history. That's also not a huge surprise, either. The juggernaut game's lavish marketing blitz took over London's Selfridges and Rockstar is even hosting an entire music festival starring a couple A-listers.

The GTA 6 Metacritic score is here, and perhaps unsurprisingly, it's not only the highest rated game of 2026, but the highest-rated game of all time.

If you look at the Metacritic "Best Games of All Time" list, there's a couple things you're going to notice – namely, Nintendo and Rockstar Games, or more specifically, Mario, Zelda, and Grand Theft Auto. And now joining GTA 4 and GTA 5 as one of the highest-rated games of all time is GTA 6, with reviews awarding it a score of 99 after 107 reviews. This makes it the highest rated game of 2026, and matches the original N64 release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever.

You just need to look at the GamesRadar+ GTA 6 review to see why, with editor-in-chief Josh West awarding the latest Rockstar Games title 5/5, saying "Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality," and adding that "there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments."

Perhaps unsurprisingly, there's a lot of outlets giving Rockstar's latest full marks, with the likes of IGN, TechRadar Gaming, Edge, and Game Informer being among the many outlets giving the max score. And as of right now there are no reviews that Metacritic classes as "Negative," or even "Mixed" for that matter.

Obviously, this Metacritic score and the game's eight nominations at The Game Awards 2026 is just the cherry on top for Rockstar, as the game is already estimated to have made $1.45 billion from pre-orders alone, and as the game releases in New Zealand right about now, I imagine that number will be far surpassed as people dig into the game.

#3834. Horu is a sci-fi 4X RTS inspired by Star Wars: Empire at War in which spaceships are spellcasters who can summon black holes

Clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously. My ears trembled beneath the trundle of a million caterpillar tracks. Balls of ice, bolts of lightning, shipments of rare alloys, and cascades of drop pods went screaming down my nerves and detonated in my frontal cortex, painting starlanes across the inside of my skull. "Oh god, they've finally found us!" I yelled, hiding beneath my desk. "I for one welcome our new galactic overlords!"

But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski. There's also a magic system, this being "the spice that makes your enemy's defeat bitter", which is a very genteel way to characterise glaciating a tank formation or conjuring a miniature blackhole.

In development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods. Horu's way of bettering Empire at War is seemingly to add a shedload more of everything. You can engage in a fleet battle that looks like two migrating ant hives colliding, even as a frankly unnecessary quantity of cyborgs pour over the forgeworld beneath and get their shit kicked in by some tornado-summoning sorcerers.

Offensives appear to work like this: any drop ships that push through the fleet battle add meat to the ground invasion, with the option of deploying wormholes to sneak your troops behind the defending armada. On the ground, you're basically out to capture control points. You're allegedly spared from "continuous babysitting" by semi-autonomous squadron commanders and an orders system that lets you queue up objectives, before units engage in battle.

You can still give individual orders to units, but that seems like a recipe for acute wrist injury. There's also a boarding action mechanic whereby your hijackers move through vessels room by room. Again, I struggle to understand how you'll have time and dexterity to oversee such skulduggery when there are a bajillion particle cannons going off all at once.

Outside of combat, there are planets to develop, shipyards to build, spy networks to groom, research trees to water, and stock markets to manipulate. It all looks like business as usual for an imperial 4X. Honestly, I can imagine the maximalist warfaring being a hot mess, and then there's the fact that the dev is running a Kickstarter "to fund the remaining assets needed for a playable build: more spaceships, more units, more animations, more sounds, more music, and everything in between." I've been burned by Kickstarter overpromising before. Still, I can only admire the vindictive intellect that would have me play a little game of FTL inside what looks like one of the larger PvP scraps from Eve Online.

You can read more on Steam. Release date there is currently none. For an equally populous strategy experience that's closer in style to Supreme Commander, check out Sanctuary: Shattered Space.

The 007 First Light score is competing with four other videogame soundtracks for the prestigious music industry trophy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The 007 First Light soundtrack, composed by Joe Henson and Alexis Leon Smith, is in the running for a Grammy award in the "Best Score Soundtrack For Videogames and Other Interactive Media" category, alongside four other contenders:

I had initially reported that the 007 First Light theme by Lana Del Rey—the one I really did not care for—was up for the award, assuming it was part of the soundtrack. It is the theme song, after all. IO Interactive later clarified that this is not the case, however: The Grammy is only for the score soundtrack, which does not include the theme song.

It seems odd to me, but that's the nature of the Grammy Awards, which are a music industry award and subject to some fairly strict rules and requirements. The rules for the videogame category, for instance, state that "videogames that contain music but are not available as stand-alone audio streams/releases" are not eligible for consideration. That means games with soundtracks that aren't released separately in some format effectively don''t exist as far as the Grammy Awards are concerned, no matter how good the music is.

The videogame soundtrack category is relatively new: The Grammy Awards only added it in 2022. Previous winners include:

#3832. Don't expect more information on The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel "for some time," Bethesda says

After Bethesda formally named The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel earlier this month, some series fans were hopeful that more news wasn't far behind. Skyrim is 15 years old today (11th November) after all, but Bethesda Game Studios has since dashed those hopes into oblivion.

In response to a Reddit post speculating about possible Sentinel news on Skyrim's birthday, the official Bethesda Game Studios account chimed in to temper everybody's expectations.

"Hey everyone, wanted to pop in to say that we aren't going to have any big announcements tomorrow," the social media account wrote. "We're excited you're excited but we will not be sharing anything new on Sentinel for some time."

The Elder Scrolls fans have already been waiting for the series' next mainline follow-up for, erm, also quite some time. Specifically, Skyrim came out in 2011, The Elder Scrolls 6's first reveal trailer reared its head in 2018, and BGS' Starfield took to the stars in 2023 - a wait so long that it had even the most faithful among us questioning if a new Elder Scrolls could ever recapture the series' magic.

So, there you have it - don't expect to see or hear about Sentinel anytime soon. Better yet, lock it up in some corner of your brain and be pleasantly surprised when it does miraculously reappear in 20XX.

In the meantime, Bethesda isn't letting Skyrim's 15th anniversary go by without a few celebrations. For one, the seminal role-playing game is deeply discounted on all platforms, in the very unlikely scenario you haven't tried it out yet.

The Elder Scrolls Online Season Two: Echoes of Skyrim is also joining the festivities by adding the Greymoor Chapter into the base game for free, giving everyone access to a few famous Skyrim locales and more. A brand-new, separate Golden Pursuit campaign will let you earn some Skyrim-centric goodies up until 2nd December, as well.

Rockstar "embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar has traditionally built its video games in a very particular way. When you're on-mission, you're treated to tightly scripted story beats designed around cinematic setpieces and very strict failure conditions. And when you're off-mission, you're free to approach situations with all of the tools at your disposal – pushing at the world until it shoves you back.

"We worked really hard on this game to blur the lines between 'on-mission' and 'off-mission' and even between types of mission," says Stephen Donkin, the vice president of design at Rockstar Games, in a statement provided to GamesRadar+.

The core missions in GTA 6 are certainly more linear by design than more free-flowing, open-world activities – like discovering the hard way that pressing Square/X whilst you are driving past a stationary police officer invites a hell of a lot more trouble than it's worth. And in case you haven't just spent over 100 hours in Leonida preparing to write a GTA 6 review, that's the button that lets Jason or Lucia shove the driver's door open to knock unsuspecting people to the ground. It's my favorite button.

Still, it's undoubtedly true that the main missions in GTA 6 offer far more flexibility than expected. Objectives are often left quite intentionally open – 'do this thing' or 'escape this area' and how you approach that really is up to you. Truth be told, a lot of this newfound flexibility isn't totally apparent on a first playthrough, revealing itself when you go back around again to try and push against the margins.

David Hynd, the vice president of technology at Rockstar, says that the team "constantly" thought about ways to bring a bit more freedom to all of the content within GTA 6 – including the missions.

"The team embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project. For example, we really wanted to reduce the number of 'Mission Fails' for the player experimenting or trying something different. And we wanted to encourage the player to do what felt right to them for their particular play style," he says.

This is undoubtedly something Rockstar has seen success with in GTA 6. And should you find yourself hitting a Mission Failed menu screen at any point, I'm also happy to report that checkpointing is majorly improved versus both GTA 5 and RDR2 – there's even the ability to Retry Checkpoint, finally.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Back to Hynd. He says that Rockstar "leveraged a lot more of our regular mechanics/AI and systems within Missions. It's a lot harder to keep Missions as open as possible (especially in a game as large as this), but the freedom and flexibility it allows the player was worth it."

As GTA 6 finally releases, Rockstar boss Sam Houser issues rare statement – "We are incredibly grateful" and "look forward to many more years of sharing these experiences with you."

#3830. Destroy All Humans remake developer goes independent, splits from THQ Nordic and parent company Embracer Group

Black Forest Games - the studio that remade the first two cult-classic Destroy All Humans games - has spun out from under former owners THQ Nordic and Embracer Group.

The Destroy All Humans remaker won its newfound independence through a management buyout, and wasted no time at all in co-founding Third Signal, which is described as a new group of independent studios that'll eventually provide help and resources to other indie teams.

"Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of 50, not 500. Black Forest Games is one of them, and the right studio to launch Third Signal. Our vision is to build a developer driven group and give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom to continue their creative legacy and bring their own ideas to life," Third Signal CEO Andreas Tobler said in a press release.

Black Forest Games was one of Embracer Group's earliest high-profile acquisitions almost a decade ago, before the company swallowed up countless big names (Lord of the Rings, Tomb Raider, Kingdom Come: Deliverance, more) in the following years and spat back a bunch shortly after. Most infamously, Embracer sold Gearbox and Borderlands during its massive internal restructuring in 2024.

It doesn't sound like Black Forest split with the rights to the Destroy All Humans series or its permanently mean alien protag Crypto, but the studio has said it's still working with THQ Nordic in some capacity. The original Destroy All Humans run nosedived wildly in quality after the second game, so I'm not sure how exciting a remake of, let's say, Destroy All Humans: Big Willy Unleashed would be nowadays, though I'd definitely be interested in seeing Crypto again in another ridiculously silly, sometimes rude and anarchic adventure.

#3829. Microsoft suffer system outage affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot, exec says there's "no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity"

Microsoft 365 isn't quite living up to its name this week, as its services have suffered an extended outage that's knocked the likes of Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for six. As of writing, the company are finally reporting "encouraging recovery progress in Europe" and are busy "addressing the remaining areas of disruption", but that's only after chunks of November 12th and 13th have seen people, businesses, and institutions left unable to use stuff they rely on.

That latest update was given by Microsoft to the BBC, who've had a live report on the outage running, since it's affected the likes of schools, government services and medical services. IGN and Kotaku's reports differ on whether any Xbox services appear to be affected. The Xbox status support page currently indicates all is swell, but Downdetector does show a recent uptick in reports of issues.

"We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue," Microsoft exec Charles LaManna wrote in response to a support thread on the topic in the early hours of November 13th UK time. "We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity."

As much as it's slightly reassuring that there currently looks to have been no big hack, the time it's taken to deploy proper fixes is concerning, with Microsoft noting some of their early attempts at rectifying things "not taking as expected".

The debacle has rather emphasised how far from ideal it is that so much key infrastructure across the world runs on one clump of tech which all go down in a heartbeat, but to a certain degree that is the peril of relying on anything. One can only hope that Microsoft's ongoing efforts to fire vast numbers of staff into the sun and embrace AI haven't factored into lots of their services going tits up for an inconvenient amount of time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A few things come to mind when I think about what the greatest fear of a Battlefield player is. It could be a glint atop the mountains on Liberation Peak, reliving the launch of Battlefield 2042, or maybe it's the randomised recoil from the first Battlefield. All of these are good bets, but I think the real shared nightmare of most Battlefield players is that someday it'll morph into Call of Duty.

To be fair, this fear isn't entirely unfounded. Bryan Beede was previously appointed as Battlefield's general manager after spending 19 years working on Call of Duty and has now been promoted to group general manager at EA. Taking his place is another Call of Duty veteran, Sam Cooper, who worked as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

"I'm excited to share that I've joined Electronic Arts as general manager of Battlefield," Cooper says in a LinkedIn post. "I started my games career at EA on the FIFA team, so coming back to where it all began feels extra special.

"Battlefield is an iconic franchise that has something no other shooter has: all-out warfare, destruction at massive scale, squads play, and a passionate community that has stuck with this franchise for more than two decades."

Now this in and of itself isn't enough to sound any alarm bells for players concerned whether or not Battlefield can stay true to form, especially since Beede was appointed as Battlefield GM back in 2021 prior to Battlefield 6's release. But this alongside some questionable new skins has some Battlefield players worried that Battlefield is becoming more "en-cod-ified".

A big talking point during Battlefield 6's launch was players begging the devs to ignore COD's trend of gimmicky skins and instead stay true to its in-game realism for cosmetics. This has largely been the case—although the Dead Space collab was a near miss. But now some believe the cracks are starting to show with the new Fox Hunter skin pack.

"There's absolutely no way you can defend this," one player says in response to the skin pack. "There's a pseudo furry skin in Battlefield now. The defense I've heard is that 'it's plausible', while these are plausible, the masks are just, no? What tactical purpose does wearing a Japanese baby mask [or] a furry mask serve?" I'd argue, however, that it could stun an enemy Battlefield player long enough for you to secure a kill, and therefore there's at least some tactical purpose to it.
